subject: Advanced Science
question: 2. Understanding Motion through Experience
answer: Understanding motion: Motion is change of position with time. Describe it by distance/displacement, time, speed, velocity and acceleration. Observe examples (walking, running, falling); quantify motion using measurements and simple formulas to compare behaviours.

subject: Advanced Science
question: 1. Compare the time taken for walking and running.
answer: For the same distance, walking takes more time than running. Measure by timing a person over a fixed distance; compare durations. Factors: fitness, slope, surface, load, and stride length affect time taken.

subject: Advanced Science
question: 2. Which motion is faster? How can you calculate speed?
answer: Running is faster. Calculate speed = distance / time (v = d/t). Use metres and seconds for m/s or kilometres and hours for km/h; average speed uses total distance divided by total time.

subject: Advanced Science
question: 3. Can motion be described using measurable quantities such as distance and time?
answer: Yes. Motion is described using measurable quantities: distance, displacement, time, speed, velocity and acceleration. These allow quantitative comparison and prediction using formulas and graphs.

subject: Advanced Science
question: 3. Newton’s Laws of Motion
answer: Newton’s three laws: 1) Inertia: a body remains at rest or uniform motion unless acted on by net force. 2) F = ma: net force equals mass times acceleration. 3) Action–reaction: every force has an equal and opposite force.

subject: Advanced Science
question: 1. Where will the boy apply force to open the door easily? (a) Near the handle (b) Near the hinges (c) At the centre of the door
answer: Answer: (a) Near the handle. Applying force farther from the hinge gives a larger torque for the same force, making the door easier to open.

subject: Advanced Science
question: 2. Why are door handles fixed far away from the hinges and not near them?
answer: Handles are far from hinges to increase the lever arm, producing greater torque for the same applied force, so doors require less effort to open.

subject: Advanced Science
question: 3. The boy applies force in a straight direction, but the door rotates. Why does this happen?
answer: The straight push produces a torque about the hinge (pivot). The hinge constrains linear motion so the applied force creates rotation (moment = force × perpendicular distance from hinge).

subject: Advanced Science
question: 4. How is it possible to rotate such a heavy object by applying force at just one end?
answer: A force at one end creates a large torque because torque = force × lever arm; long arms give mechanical advantage. Bearings/hinges reduce friction, so a modest force can rotate a heavy object.

subject: Advanced Science
question: 5. Work and Energy
answer: Work is force times displacement in the force direction: W = F·d·cosθ. Energy is the capacity to do work (kinetic, potential, thermal). Work transfers or converts energy; total energy is conserved in closed systems.

subject: Advanced Science
section: Activity 5.2 (Spring - Force vs Extension Graph Task)
question: 1. Prepare a graph between Force and extension in the spring with the help of data observed in the activity by taking X-axis → Extension (m or cm) Y-axis → Force (N) Reflect on the Following (Friction and Non-Conservative Forces)
answer: Plot extension (x-axis) vs force (y-axis). Draw points, connect—Hooke’s law gives a straight line through origin until elastic limit; slope = spring constant k (N/m). Reflection: friction/non-conservative forces convert mechanical energy to heat, reducing recoverable energy.

subject: Advanced Science
section: Activity 5.2 (Spring - Force vs Extension Graph Task)
question: 1. If there were no friction, would a moving object ever stop?
answer: No friction means no dissipative force; in ideal Newtonian mechanics a moving object continues indefinitely at constant velocity unless acted on by another force (it would not stop).

subject: Advanced Science
section: Activity 5.2 (Spring - Force vs Extension Graph Task)
question: 2. Why do pendulums slowly stop after some time?
answer: Pendulums stop because air resistance and pivot friction dissipate mechanical energy into heat and sound, gradually reducing amplitude until motion ceases.

subject: Advanced Science
section: Activity 5.2 (Spring - Force vs Extension Graph Task)
question: 3. Why do machines require lubrication?
answer: Lubrication reduces friction and wear between moving parts, lowers heat generation and energy loss, prevents corrosion, and prolongs machine life and efficiency.

subject: Advanced Science
section: Activity 5.2 (Spring - Force vs Extension Graph Task)
question: 9. Microscope and Microscopy
answer: Microscope basics: instruments magnify small objects using lenses or electron beams. Light microscopes show cells and tissues; electron microscopes give much higher resolution for organelles and microbes. Key concepts: magnification and resolution.

subject: Advanced Science
question: 1. Draw a horizontal line. Mark at least 5 important dates in microscopy and add a tiny sketch or symbol for each (e.g., cork cells, bacteria, electron beam etc.).
answer: Timeline (horizontal): 1590 – early compound microscope (Janssen) [sketch: simple tube]; 1665 – Hooke: cork cells (book/cork sketch); 1670s – Leeuwenhoek: bacteria (tiny dots); 1830s – improved achromatic lenses (lens symbol); 1931 – electron microscope (beam symbol).

subject: Advanced Science
question: 10. Engineering Life - Miracles in Biotechnology
answer: Engineering Life: biotechnology uses living systems to make products—fermentation, genetic engineering, CRISPR, bioreactors and diagnostics. It solves health/agricultural problems but requires ethical, safety and regulatory oversight.

subject: Advanced Science
section: Activity 10.1 (Observe Fermentation at Home - Discussion Questions)
question: 1. In what times or situations does curd take a long time to form?
answer: Curd formation is slow when ambient temperature is low, starter culture is weak/old, milk is very hot or cold, container is unclean, or milk is highly diluted/contaminated with antibacterial agents.

subject: Advanced Science
section: Activity 10.1 (Observe Fermentation at Home - Discussion Questions)
question: 2. What conditions support the curdling of milk? Think and Discuss (Ethical Principles)
answer: Curdling needs lactic acid bacteria, warm temperature (about 30–40°C), fresh milk, a clean container, and proper starter quantity. Avoid extreme heat, cold, or antiseptic contamination.

subject: Advanced Science
section: Activity 10.1 (Observe Fermentation at Home - Discussion Questions)
question: 1. There are four important ethical principles that help evaluate the impact of biotechnology on society. These principles act as guidelines to understand the benefits, risks and fairness related to emerging biotechnologies. The figure shows different modern biotechnologies placed under four ethical principles: Beneficence (Doing Good) Non -maleficence (Do Not Harm) Autonomy (Freedom of Choice) Justice and Fairness Each emerging biotechnology has been grouped under the principle wh ere ethical concerns may arise. (SynBio refers to Synthetic Biolog y.)
answer: Four ethical principles: Beneficence—do good; Non-maleficence—avoid harm; Autonomy—respect choices; Justice—fairness in benefits/risks. Use these to evaluate biotech impacts, balancing innovation, safety, consent and equitable access.

question: 2. The Stage Is Yours
answer: Stage preparation: pick a clear theme, assign director/actors/crew, create simple blocking and props, rehearse scenes with timing and cues, refine acting choices and audience engagement, and do technical run-throughs.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Form Your Theatre Team - Design a Logo
question: 1. Activity 2.1. Activity 2.1 Logo artwork: Create your team's logo by making a few sketches. Keep your design simple so that it can be easily replicated. Select colours for your logo such that they enhance the ideas you wish to communicate. Create the final artwork of your logo. Your team's name can be a part of the logo or be placed alongside.

answer: Notice elements: masks (drama/characters), lines (movement/direction), colours (mood), symbols (books/tree/torch). They represent your team’s focus—story type, values, energy, and what you want audiences to feel.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)

question: 2. Discuss the following prompts as you design your logo: What does theatre mean to you? What do you believe in? What is your team about? What kind of stories do you want to tell? What do you want your audience to experience? Process of Making Purposeful Theatre
answer: Sample answers: Theatre means storytelling and shared experience. We believe in empathy and honest stories. Our team tells social, human stories. We want audiences to feel moved, think, and laugh. Simplicity and resourcefulness guide our choices.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)

Examine the responses through the following questions: What emotions and themes emerged from the interaction? What surprised you? How can the information help you write a story on this topic?
answer: Collect responses, list recurring emotions/themes, note surprises and contradictions. Use prominent emotions as story spine, develop characters embodying themes, and shape scenes that reveal causes and consequences of those feelings.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)

question: 2. Let us recall: Refer to Chapter 2 of the Grade 8 Art Education textbook Kriti to recall the different types of scripts, dramatic structures, and genres. Which stage props, costumes, and character make-up will help you tell your story best? How can you best use the resources around you? How will your team assign backstage responsibilities?

question: 4. Creativity in Light and Sound
answer: Light and sound creativity: pick colour and intensity to set mood, direction for shape and shadow, and matching soundscape. Synchronize cues, use contrasts, and keep changes purposeful to enhance emotional beats and focus.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 4.1 - Making a Simple Spotlight and Gobo
question: 1. Activity 4.1. Activity 4.1 Making a simple spotlight and gobo: In groups of 5-6 students, make one spotlight and gobo. Materials (per group): 1 torch or flashlight or phone torch; Black chart paper; Thick black paper or thin cardboard; Tape and scissors. Making a spotlight: 1. Wrap the black chart paper near the source of light of the torch or flashlight like a tube. This should prevent light from any leak or spread. Attach it securely to the torch or flashlight using a tape. 2. Switch on the torch and observe how the tube narrows and focuses the beam. Making a simple gobo: 1. Draw a simple shape or pattern on a black paper (tree branches, window bars, rain lines, stars, etc.). 2. Carefully cut out the shapes, like a stencil (the teacher to assist). 3. Tape the cut-out in front of the spotlight tube. Adjust the distance between the light source and gobo to get sharp shadows. 4. Shine the light onto a wall. You will now see patterned light. Performance challenge: Each group must create a 1-minute scene using the gobo image as the centre of the scene. For example, if your gobo is that of a tree, create a scene about how a woodcutter comes to cut the tree for timber, but a child stops him and protects the tree. Activity 4.2 - Design the Moment
answer: Spotlight/gobo method: build tube around torch, cut a stencil gobo, tape in front, adjust distance for sharpness. Sample 1‑minute scene: gobo = tree silhouette; action: woodcutter approaches, child pleads, community intervenes; use torch, shadow puppets, a chopping sound.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 4.1 - Making a Simple Spotlight and Gobo
question: 1. Activity 4.2. Activity 4.2 'Design the moment' - A light and sound simulation exercise. Materials Needed: Different light sources (torches, phone flashlight, bulbs); Coloured transparent sheets (or paper of different colours); Speakers or classroom audio system; Everyday classroom objects - stationery, water bottle, bag, or lunch box; Simple stick puppets (details in the 'Theatre' section in Grade 6 textbook Kriti); A set of short dramatic situations. Process: 1. The teacher introduces a 10-15 second dramatic situation. For example: A lost child in a forest; A hero discovering a hidden treasure; and A magical door opening. 2. Students work in small groups to discuss the following: Which colour light best suits the mood? Which direction should the light come from (top, side, front)? What sound would accompany the moment? How to plan the scene using bags, water bottles, and other classroom objects as props and puppets in place of actors? For example, the water bottle could represent a tree, and a pen and small pencil could be a parent walking with a child. (As learnt under object improvisation in previous grades.) Puppets may also be used to represent the parent and child. 3. One student in each group holds the torch covered with a coloured sheet and points it in the chosen direction towards the small object on their desk (such as a pen or notebook) to simulate stage lighting. 4. Another student plays the selected sound clip from a phone or laptop. 5. The group presents their 'designed moment' to the class, explaining why they chose those particular lights and sounds.
answer: Design-the-moment sample (lost child): choose dim blue top light for eerie mood, soft rustling/heartbeat sound, water bottle as tree, pen as parent. One student lights, another plays sound; present 10–15s tableau and explain choices.

question: 5. From Vision to Performance: Direction and Acting
answer: From vision to performance: director clarifies concept, guides blocking, shapes actors’ objectives, times cues with lighting/sound, runs focused rehearsals, gives constructive feedback, and coordinates tech and final dress rehearsals.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 5.1. Activity 5.1 The director in you: Pick a scene of your choice from a play you have performed. Make groups of 5 - 10 (depending on the scenes). Each team will re-design the scene using the ideas below. Focus on the following techniques: 1. Emphasise more on movements or angika. 2. Focus more on the vachika, or voice elements. 3. Re-work the positions and movements based on the nine parts of the stage. 4. Enact a scene without any emotions. Do you feel you have more ideas to explore? Go ahead and explore more possibilities. There is no end to your creativity. Enact the scenes and discuss how different the impact was. Activity 5.2 - The Living Painting
answer: Choose one scene you performed. Re-design in four versions: (a) Angika-focused — exaggerate body, gestures, dynamics; (b) Vachika-focused — alter voice, pitch, pace, pauses; (c) Stage-division — re-block using nine parts for balance and sightlines; (d) No-emotion — neutral delivery. Enact each and note differences in clarity, audience empathy, and rhythm.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 5.2. Activity 5.2 The living painting. Instructions: 1. Divide the class into small groups. 2. Each group chooses a famous painting, sculpture, or traditional artwork. 3. The task: Bring the artwork to life as a short 1-minute performance! Steps for each group: 1. Pick a painting, sculpture, or traditional artwork from the textbook. 2. Imagine a possible situation for the picture. What might have happened before, and what might have happened after. Create a small story with that character or place as the core. 3. Direction: Discuss and plan the positions for each character based on their importance and the stage divisions you have learnt. Plan the entry and exit of characters as per the story and stage divisions. 4. Acting: The actors turn the still image into a living moment using expression, movement, and maybe even short lines of dialogue or sound. Is the situation familiar to you in any way? Can you bring that to your performance? Try enacting the entire scene only with angika, without speech. Try a vachika version where the actors only speak in their position without any actions or gestures. Add music, rhythm, or dance to enrich the scene. Each group presents their 'living painting' to the class. Activity 5.3 - Solo to Ensemble
answer: Divide into groups, pick a known artwork (e.g., The Last Supper or a local folk painting). Create before/after story, assign positions by importance and stage divisions, plan entries/exits. Perform: angika-only, vachika-only, add music/dance. Debrief on which choices brought the image alive.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 5.3. Activity 5.3 Solo to ensemble. Step 1: Solo presence - A single student walks onto the stage and performs a simple action silently (for example, waiting for a bus, tying a shoelace, searching for something lost). Other students observe posture, energy, clarity of action. Discussion: What helped the students understand what the actor was doing without words? Step 2: Group dynamic - In groups of 5-6, perform the same situation on stage (for example, everyone is waiting at a bus stop). No one is the main character. Students must listen with their eyes and bodies, adjust spacing, rhythm, and reactions. Discussion: Who leads unintentionally? How does one actor's energy affect the whole group? Step 3: Disruption and balance (5 minutes) - The teacher asks one actor to deliberately change the tempo or emotion (for example, becoming restless or slow). The group must organically adjust without speaking. Discussion Circle - Solo and Group Dynamics in Acting
answer: Step 1: Solo: perform a silent action; observers note posture, intent, clarity. Step 2: Group: reproduce scenario, equal focus, adapt spacing and rhythm. Step 3: Disruption: one actor changes tempo; others adjust nonverbally. Discuss leadership, cueing, and collective responsiveness.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Discussion circle: Discuss the difference in impact between the angika and vachika versions.
answer: Angika emphasizes visual storytelling — immediate, universal, physical clarity. Vachika uses vocal colour, rhythm, subtext and nuance. Angika impacts through movement and image; vachika adds internal life, subtext and emotional layers. Combined they amplify meaning.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 2. Discussion circle: How did acting solo feel different from acting in a group? Project Work
answer: Solo acting centers focus, clarity, and inner choice control. Group acting requires listening, spatial awareness, shared timing and democratic energy. Solo feels intimate and controlled; group feels organic, unpredictable, and dependent on others' energies.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Project Work 1. Planning and Conducting a Basic Workshop. Objective: To help Grade 9 students deepen their understanding of theatre by planning and conducting a three-hour theatre workshop for younger students (Grades 3 - 5), working in pairs. This not only develops a deeper understanding of the concepts learnt so far, but also builds leadership, communication, planning, empathy, and practical theatre skills. Possible Workshop Themes: Each team of two to decide on a theme to plan their workshop session. 1. Storytelling through body and voice 2. Emotions and expressions on stage 3. Animals, nature and movement 4. Creating characters from everyday life 5. The magic of imagination in theatre 6. Folk stories and simple drama 7. Rhythm, sound, and movement games 8. Teamwork and trust through theatre games. Suggested 3-Hour Structure: Hour 1: Warm-up and comfort; Hour 2: Core theatre activities; Hour 3: Creation and sharing. Planning Steps: Step 1: Divide roles; Step 2: Know your audience; Step 3: Design activities; Step 4: Prepare materials; Step 5: Rehearse as facilitators and plan backup activities; Step 6: Reflection after workshop - Hold a discussion circle with the children to get their thoughts. After the workshop, have a mutual discussion - what worked well? What was challenging? Reflect on what you have learnt as a theatre facilitator?
answer: Two students plan a 3-hour workshop: Hour 1 warm-ups and icebreakers; Hour 2 core activities (body/voice/emotion games) tied to chosen theme; Hour 3 simple creation and sharing. Divide facilitator roles, prepare materials, rehearse, keep backups, and hold reflection with children and co-facilitator.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 6. Music and Us
answer: ‘Music and Us’ explores daily music practices: listening, making playlists, family songs, and mapping regional traditions. Activities: journaling, interviews, live listening, and reflective sharing to connect music with identity and well-being.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 6.1. Activity 6.1 My music journal: Keep a journal dedicated to music, which you will maintain over Grades 9 and 10. In this journal, you will chronicle the songs that you listen to, learn, and create. You will also use it to document the various creative exercises you do. Musical texts and treatises often have creative names. What would you like to name your journal? Write your journal name in a decorative manner on the cover page. Activity 6.2 - Listening to Various Genres
answer: Pick a creative title (examples: ‘SwarSanchay’, ‘TuneTrove’). Decorate the cover with symbols of music (notes, instruments). Use dated entries: song name, date, source, activity (learned/created), reflections and practice notes across Grades 9–10.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 6.2. Activity 6.2 Listening to various genres: When you listen to a piece of music, write the name of the song and tick the genre. By the end of the year, try and listen to various genres of music. Hindustani vocal; Carnatic vocal; Carnatic instrumental; Hindustani instrumental; Indian pop; Others; Folk song; Patriotic; Film song; World music; Devotional Activity 6.3 - Identify the Genre of Music
answer: When you hear a piece, record: song name, artist, date, then tick genre(s) from the list. Note identifying features (scale, rhythm, instrumentation, language). Aim to sample many genres across the year and mark each listening entry.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 6.3. Activity 6.3 Identify the genre of music: Listen to the song played by your teacher in class. Discuss the points given below. Write the details of the song in your journal. Identify its genre. Which of its features helped you identify it? Identify the musical instruments in this piece of music. Try and describe the sound of that instrument in words. Identify the musicians who are singing or playing on this track. Is there something characteristic about their voice or style of singing/ playing? Try and describe how listening to the song made you feel. If you could change something about the song, what would it be, and why? Activity 6.4 - Creating My Playlist
answer: To identify genre: listen for scale/raga, rhythmic pattern, instruments, vocal style and language. List instruments heard and describe timbre (bright, nasal, resonant). Note singers/players and characteristic techniques. Record emotional effect and one suggested change with reason.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 6.4. Activity 6.4 Creating my playlist: A playlist is a group of songs that are put together for a reason, either by a listener, an artist, or a music platform. Playlists can be based on the theme of the song, like 'songs about rain', the type of music, like 'Indipop playlist', or even the reason they are listened to, like 'music while studying'. A playlist is not just a collection of songs, but can also be a tool to mirror and balance our emotions. In your journal, create a playlist of around five songs. Give your playlist a name, she has 'My mood uplifter', or 'Songs to make me calm'. For each song, mention the following: 1. Name of the song 2. Genre 3. Raga and tala (if a classical song) 4. Composer and lyricist 5. Artists: Singer/ instrumentalists/ band name 6. Why I like the song 7. I listen to this song when I am feeling Activity 6.5 - Songs and Traditional Knowledge
answer: Create a playlist page template: 1) Playlist name; 2) For each song: Name | Genre | Raga/Tala (if applicable) | Composer/lyricist | Artists | Why I like it | When I listen. Example entry: ‘My Mood Uplifter’ — “Jai Ho” | Film/Pop | — | A.R. Rahman | Singer: Sukhwinder Singh | Energetic, celebratory — when I need energy.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 6.5. Activity 6.5 Songs and traditional knowledge: Find recordings of these songs online, listen to them and sing along. You can also invite a group of musicians in your vicinity and let the children learn the song. What are the community traditions and practices that are documented in this song? Can you think of a similar song from your region? Compare it with the song given on the preceding page. Activity 6.6 - Mapping Regional Music Traditions
answer: Find recordings, listen and learn by singing along or inviting local musicians. Note community traditions referenced, performance context, instruments, occasions. Compare with a similar regional song: list similarities (form, lyrics, function) and differences (melody, rhythm, language).

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 6.6. Activity 6.6 Mapping regional music traditions: Draw a map of our country in your journal. Recall the various folk music forms that you have heard or learnt previously. Mark the various folk music forms in the region they are found in. This will help you understand how every region has different genres and communities which practice a variety of musical traditons. Activity 6.7 - My Family Tradition
answer: Draw India’s outline, mark folk forms where they belong (e.g., Bhangra—Punjab; Baul—West Bengal; Lavani—Maharashtra). Add brief notes on instruments and occasions. Use class/wider research to fill gaps and colour-code similar genres.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 6.7. Activity 6.7 My family tradition: Families often have traditions relating to festivals, rituals, recipes, etc., that are shared across generations. Speak to your parents, grandparents, or elders and ask them about your family traditions or recipes. Pick one tradition or family recipe that you would like to conserve. Write the lyrics of a song based on the information. Take inspiration from the various song structures that you observed in Activity 6.3. Once you have written your song, sing it in a tune of your choice. You now have your own family song! Share it with your family during the next festival or gathering.
answer:
Interview elders about one tradition/recipe. Extract key lines and craft a short family song. Example (Hindi, 2 lines):
"घर की खुशबू, दादी का तड़का, गीतों में बसी यादें; सदा साथ चलें ये हवा, बाँटें हम सुख-दुःख के सालें." Sing to a simple tune and share.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 7. The Science of Music
answer: The science of music links breath (diaphragm, lungs), vibration (larynx, vocal folds), and resonance (throat, mouth, nasal cavities, instrument bodies). Observe pitch, timbre, and acoustics; simple experiments: change tube length, compare resonances, note waveform differences.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 7.3 - Experiencing the Human Vocal System
question: 1. Activity 7.3. Activity 7.3 Experiencing the human vocal system: Place your hands on your belly. Take a big breath in, and notice your belly expand outwards. Now, exhale and notice how your belly moves inwards. (Air pressure system - Diaphragm, lungs, and surrounding muscles) Try the same activity again, but this time, as you exhale, make a soft mmmm sound; experience the connection between the breath and the voice. (Vibratory system - Voice box (larynx) and vocal folds (or vocal cords)) Do the same activity, but this time, as you make a sound, first start with mmmmm and then vary the shape of your mouth to make various sounds like aaaa, oooo, eeee and uuuuu. (Resonating system - Throat, mouth, nasal cavities) Activity 7.4 - Daily Vocal Warm-up Routine
answer: Hands-on steps: place hands on belly, inhale — feel outward expansion; exhale — feel inward. Exhale while humming (mmmm) to sense vibration. Change vowel shapes (aaaa, oooo, eeee, uuuu) and notice shifts in resonance location and timbre.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 7.3 - Experiencing the Human Vocal System
question: 1. Activity 7.4. Activity 7.4 Daily vocal warm-up routine (Practise each exercise 5-6 times.): 1. Breathing and Diaphragm Exercise - Stand or sit straight. Inhale deeply through the nose, letting your lungs expand (Grade 7 Chapter 9 Science textbook). Hold for 2-3 seconds, then exhale slowly through the mouth. Benefits: Activates lungs and diaphragm, extending breath control while singing long phrases for better control and supports long phrases in singing. 2. Humming (Bhramari pranayama) - Hum a note at a comfortable pitch, feeling the vibration in the lips, nose, and chest. Gently slide up and down in pitch while saying mmm. Benefits: Warms up vocal cords gently and improves resonance. 3. Lip Trills/ Bubbles - Blow air through closed lips while making a sound like a brrr or the sound of a motorbike. Glide up and down in pitch using the lip trill. Benefits: Relaxes facial muscles, reduces tension, improves airflow. 4. Sargam exercises - Sing alankara patterns in varying speeds to improve vocal control: i. SGR, RMG, GPM (complete the pattern) ii. SRGM, RGMP, GMPD (complete the pattern). See how many phrases you can sing in one breath. As you practise these exercises regularly, you may notice that you can sing longer phrases in a single breath. Benefits: Improves voice flexibility and breath control
answer: Daily routine (5–6 times each): 1) Deep diaphragmatic breaths (3–5 breaths); 2) Humming slides (Bhramari) warming resonance; 3) Lip trills across pitch range; 4) Sargam/alankara patterns at varying speeds to build flexibility and breath control.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 7.3 - Experiencing the Human Vocal System
question: 8. Raga and Tala
answer: Raga = melodic framework (notes, ascent/descent, mood). Tala = rhythmic cycle with stressed sam. Study tips: learn one raga and one tala deeply; practise sargam with tala, listen to recordings, and mark sam and vibhags while clapping/tapping.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 8.2. Activity 8.2 Identifying the various bols: Listen to a recording of the theka being played on the tabla and try and identify its bols.
answer: Listen to theka recordings, slow audio if needed, and transcribe bols by ear (e.g., dha, dhin, na, tin). Note recurring patterns and bols per measure. Practice clapping theka while reciting bols to internalize sound-to-syllable mapping.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 8.3. Activity 8.3 Finding sam: Try and follow along the tabla theko of the bandish being played in class and identify the sam as you follow the tala. Observe how the artist, in their elaboration, arrives at the sam in different ways.
answer: Follow the bandish theka, feel the cyclic return point (sam) as the strongest beat. Mark it physically (clap or stand), observe how artists return to sam via cadence, ornamentation or phrase ending. Practice predicting sam during improvisations.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 8.4. Activity 8.4 Listening to a song and identifying the tala pattern: As you listen to the song, first react naturally to the beat by tapping your feet, clapping your hand, etc. Now, try and find how many beats this tala cycle has.
answer: React naturally to beat (tap/clap), then group beats into repeating cycles until pattern repeats. Count beats per cycle to identify tala (e.g., 8 — Teen Taal, 16 — Teentaal variants). Confirm by listening for stressed sam and vibhag divisions.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 8.6. Activity 8.6 Fitting your song to tala: Go back to the song you created in Chapter 6 Activity 6.7 (My family tradition). Does your song naturally fall into a tala or rhythm pattern? How will you modify it (by speeding it up, slowing it down, elongating or compressing a syllable, or adding or removing a word) to fit it to a specific rhythm pattern? Try singing or reciting your song while keeping a tala/ steady beat. How does this change the feel of your song?
answer: Check if your family song fits a tala by tapping steady beats and aligning syllables. Modify by lengthening/shortening syllables, adding filler words, or shifting accents. Sing with tala; note how rhythm changes mood and phrasing, then choose preferred version.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 13. Dance Choreography
answer: Dance choreography explores spatial formations, timing, motifs, dynamics, and interaction. Key fundamentals: counts, entrances/exits, symmetry/asymmetry, focal points, and how movement vocabulary conveys theme and emotion.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 13.1. Activity 13.1 Plan a choreography: Using the diagrams of a stage with markings as shown above, plot where different dancers can position themselves to create different formations. You can choose the number of dancers you would like in your choreography. This can also be done physically with dancers in your space. Activity 13.2 - Creating Your Choreography
answer: Use a stage diagram, mark nine parts. For five dancers: D1 centre front (lead), D2 stage left front, D3 stage right front, D4 upstage left, D5 upstage right. Plan entrances/exits, diagonals, lines, circles, and focal switches for variety.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 13.2. Activity 13.2 Creating your choreography: Divide yourself into four groups. Choose your lead choregrapher. First, each choreographer creates a solo movement portraying a concept of their choice (for example, contemporary theme, or depiction of nature like rain and thunderstorms, or celebration of festivals, etc.). They may choose any movement vocabulary they are comfortable with. Next, each lead choreographer must adapt their solo phrase into a group choreography, exploring formations, spacing, timing, and interaction. The choreography can include aspects of all four abhinayas, such as: expressive, stylised movements (use of hand gestures, animation, and mime); rhythmic syllables and spoken word; props; and emotional expression. Each solo choreographer presents their choreography, followed by the group performance of the same. Observe each group's performance and explore how it can change and how expression changes with group interaction and usage of space in a: solo performance; and group performance Activity 13.3 - Reflections
answer: Each choreographer creates a short solo motif, then expands it for group: assign roles, explore formations, sync counts, add props/music. Rehearse transitions and dynamics. Perform solo then group; observe how interaction changes expression and clarity.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 13.3. Activity 13.3 Reflections: Reflect on and analyse the choreography created in Activity 13.2. Review your performance and ask for feedback from your peers and experts. Record it in your dance journal. Self-Review: Were you able to communicate your concept clearly through your choreography? What worked well? Peer Review: Observe the feedback given by your peers and discuss amongst yourselves. Expert Review: Take supportive and constructive feedback from your teacher or an invited expert on the clarity, creativity, and effectiveness of your work. Activity 13.4 - Well-being Discussion Circle
answer: Self-review: Did choreography convey concept? What succeeded? Peer review: note strengths and actionable suggestions. Expert review: ask about clarity, creativity, structure. Record feedback and planned revisions in dance journal.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 13.4. Activity 13.4 Well-being discussion circle. Prompts may include the following: Now that you have completed your journey with dance and movement this year, discuss your experiences and observations of the various concepts you have learnt and practised. Reflect on your experiences of creating, sharing, and collaborating. End the circle by identifying your silver lining! Find something positive you discovered about yourself, your group, and the creative process.
answer: Discussion prompts: What surprised you? What creative skill improved? How did collaboration feel? Name one personal ‘silver lining’ (e.g., improved confidence, listening, or leadership). Share one intention for future practice.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 14. Exploring the Fundamentals of Visual Arts
answer: Visual fundamentals cover line, shape, form, colour, texture, value, and space. Explore each through daily exercises, observation, and journals. Combine elements to build compositions and reflect on choices and effects.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 14.1 - Explore Artists' Journals in Groups
question: 1. Activity 14.1. Activity 14.1 Explore artists' journals in groups. Step 1: Make five groups. Step 2: Use books or digital resources to search for artists' journals. You could also choose from the examples given in Fig. 14.1. Leonardo Da Vinci's notebooks; Frida Kahlo's diary; Rabindranath Tagore's doodles; Painting of birds and animals by Ustad Mansur; Nandalal Bose's illustration. Step 3: Share your findings about how visual artists recorded various experiences and ideas in their journals. Activity 14.2 - Apply the Elements of Art
answer: Form five groups, research artists’ journals (Da Vinci sketches, Frida’s diary, Tagore’s doodles, Mansur’s studies). Share findings: how journals capture ideas, experiments, observations, and development. Note uses: studies, references, and creative seeds.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 14.1 - Explore Artists' Journals in Groups
question: 1. Activity 14.2. Activity 14.2 Apply the elements of art: The elements of art are basic components that are used to create a visual artwork. Dedicate a page in your journal for each of the seven elements of art. Create the element in many varieties using different materials. Create designs and patterns, and fill the entire page. Day - Element - Mediums and Techniques - Suggestions: 1. Point - Pencils, pens, sketch pens, markers - Make dots of varying sizes. 2. Line - Pencils, pens, colour pencils, crayons, pastels, charcoal, chalk - Draw curvy, wavy, zigzag, dotted, dashed, and other types of lines in varying thickness. 3. Shape and Form - Pencils, pens, markers, crayons, paints - Doodle and create different shapes. Add light and shade to create a three-dimensional form. 4. Texture - Collage, frottage - Collect and paste textured materials. Create rubbings of textured surfaces and objects. 5. Colour - Crayons, colour pencils, water colours, poster colours - Play with blotches of colour in different mediums. 6. Value - Crayons, colour pencils, water colours, poster colours - Create colour tints, tones, and shades to show value. 7. Space - Any of the above mediums - Draw lines to demarcate the space on the page in interesting ways. Play with positive and negative space. Activity 14.3 - Daily Sketching Schedule
answer: Dedicate one page per element across a week. Example schedule: Day 1 Point — dot studies; Day 2 Line — varied strokes; Day 3 Shape/Form — shaded forms; Day 4 Texture — frottage/collage; Day 5 Colour — swatches; Day 6 Value — tints/shades; Day 7 Space — foreground/background exercises.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 14.1 - Explore Artists' Journals in Groups
question: 1. Activity 14.3. Activity 14.3 Daily sketching schedule: The table below can help you schedule regular sketching with weekly targets. Aim to spend more than the minimum time mentioned here. Note: Sketch in your journal or on any paper which you can later paste into your journal. Write the date, time, and place. Minimum time per sketch - Themes - Sketches per day: 5 minutes - Objects in your school or home - 2; 10 minutes - Plants/ landscapes in your school/ home - 2; 10 minutes - Animals, insects, birds, and other life forms in your natural surroundings - 1; 10 minutes - Different actions/ postures - 2; 15 minutes - Buildings and architectural details - 1. Weekly target - 8 sketches Activity 14.4 - Apply the Principles of Visual Design
answer: Sample daily plan: Morning (7:00) — two 10-min plant/landscape sketches; Mid-morning (10:30) — two 5-min object sketches; Afternoon (4:00) — one 10-min animal/insect sketch; Evening (6:00) — two 10-min action/posture sketches. Do one 15-min building twice weekly. Always write date, time, and place in your journal. Weekly target: 8+ sketches.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 14.1 - Explore Artists' Journals in Groups
question: 1. Activity 14.4. Activity 14.4 Apply the principles of visual design: 1. Revise the principles of visual design - The principles of visual design are important concepts that help us improve the aesthetic qualities of artworks. These principles guide the structure, arrangement, and overall composition of visual elements. The six principles you will examine are: unity and harmony; balance; rhythm and movement; emphasis; proportion; and hierarchy (order of importance). 2. Observe and analyse the principles of design in printed material around you, including textbooks of other subjects. 3. Make three to four entries in your journal guided by these prompts: Look through old newspapers and magazines for interesting designs. You will find them in brand promotions, logos, advertisements, fashion photography, book cover designs, food wrappers, etc. You can also collect textile scraps and discarded food wrappers. Cut out designs that interest you and analyse the principles of design. Mention the principles that you observe in the design. You can also cut out examples that you think are not well-designed and analyse their problems.
answer: How to make 3–4 journal entries: 1) Collect cut-outs (ads, covers, wrappers). 2) Paste each example and note observed principles (unity, balance, rhythm, emphasis, proportion, hierarchy). 3) For poor designs, list problems (clutter, weak focal point, bad contrast) and suggest fixes.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 14.1 - Explore Artists' Journals in Groups
question: 15. Mediums and Techniques in Visual Art
answer: Mediums and techniques: Common mediums include pencil, charcoal, ink, watercolour, acrylic, oil, pastels, clay, wood, metal, textiles, printmaking, photography, and digital. Techniques: sketching, glazing, impasto, carving, modelling, casting, weaving, collage, and mixed media approaches.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 15.1 - Which Mediums Are You Interested In?
question: 1. Activity 15.1. Activity 15.1: Which mediums are you interested in? Note down a list of all the mediums mentioned above. Try to find the ones that are easily available and use them in your artwork. Activity 15.2 - Find Out About Indian Sculptural Crafts
answer: List of accessible mediums: pencil, charcoal, coloured pencils, crayons, watercolours, acrylics, gouache, poster colours, clay (air-dry), fabric scraps, cardboard, and simple printing (potato/stamp). Try pencils, watercolours, clay, and collage first — they are easy and affordable.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 15.1 - Which Mediums Are You Interested In?
question: 1. Activity 15.2. Activity 15.2 Find out about any two Indian sculptural crafts: Use these prompts and write a one-page report in your journal that includes drawings/ photos. Name the art tradition and region where it is practised. Name an artist who practices it, if known. Mention the materials and mediums used. Describe the technique or process. Mention the source of your information. Activity 15.3 - Handcraft a Three-Dimensional Object
answer: Two Indian sculptural crafts (brief): 1) Dokra (West Bengal/Chhattisgarh) — lost-wax brass casting; artists: Dhokra craftsmen; materials: wax, clay, brass; process: wax model → clay mould → melt wax → pour molten metal. 2) Kondapalli toys (Andhra Pradesh) — softwood carving and tempera painting; artists: Kondapalli artisans; materials: Tella Poniki wood, natural colours; process: carve, assemble, paint. (Verify sources: craft websites, local museums.)

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 15.1 - Which Mediums Are You Interested In?
question: 1. Activity 15.3. Activity 15.3 Handcraft a three-dimensional object: Choose easily available materials like clay, fabric, natural fibres, or soft wood. Your artwork can be a functional object like a pen stand, decoration for the home, headgear, jewellery, etc. Explore traditional materials and processes that would be suitable. Plan your process and create your artwork. Innovate on your own if you are working without an expert's guidance. Display your artwork and share your experiences with others. Activity 15.4 - Make a Mixed Media Colour Wheel
answer: Making a clay pen stand (example): Materials: air-dry clay, water, cutting tool, sandpaper, paint. Steps: plan shape; roll and join clay pieces; smooth joins; add holes; air-dry 24–48 hrs; sand and paint; varnish optional. Display and note challenges and innovations in your journal.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 15.1 - Which Mediums Are You Interested In?
question: 1. Activity 15.4. Activity 15.4 Make a mixed media colour wheel: Make a colour wheel with the primary, secondary, and tertiary colours. Use a variety of mediums in your colour wheel - pencils, crayons, pens, markers, collage with printed matter, pasting fabric scraps, and other materials. Map the warm and cool colours. Practise making tints, shades, and tones of different colours. Looking at Fig. 15.7, map the complementary and analogous colours on your colour wheel. Activity 15.5 - Mark the Vanishing Point and Draw Converging Lines
answer: Make a mixed-media colour wheel: Draw a circle divided into 12 segments. Fill primaries (red, blue, yellow), secondaries (orange, green, purple), tertiaries. Use varied materials (pencil, pastel, fabric, magazine collage). Mark warm/cool halves, practice tints (add white), shades (add black), and tones (add grey). Label complementary and analogous pairs.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 15.1 - Which Mediums Are You Interested In?
question: 1. Activity 15.5. Activity 15.5 Mark the vanishing point and draw converging lines: In Fig. 15.9, the lines in the architecture converge at the centre of the painting where Aristotle and Plato are surrounded by a gathering of philosophers, scientists, and mathematicians, which include Socrates, Pythagoras, Archimedes, Heraclitus, and many others. Find out more about the painting on the internet with your teacher's help. Use a pencil to mark the vanishing point on this painting. Draw the lines below eye level and above eye level, which converge at the vanishing point. Activity 15.7 - Create an Artwork Using Perspective Techniques
answer: Method to mark vanishing point on the painting (e.g., The School of Athens): Find the central architectural convergence point online with your teacher. Use a ruler to draw several straight guides from lower and upper edges toward that point; these are converging lines. Note: exact lines depend on the supplied figure.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 15.1 - Which Mediums Are You Interested In?
question: 1. Activity 15.7. Activity 15.7 Create an artwork using perspective techniques. Size of artwork: Approximately A4. Take inspiration from the Deccan miniature painting to re-imagine dancers from your life and time. Create an artwork depicting dancers and apply the techniques of linear perspective and aerial perspective. Do not copy the miniature painting. Step 1: Recall dance forms you have seen around you and visualise a scene of two or more people dancing together. Step 2: Visualise their postures, actions, expressions, costumes, and jewellery. Step 3: Choose either an indoor or outdoor setting with some architectural elements like your school building, a wedding venue, a street, a monument, etc. Be imaginative! Step 4: Make a sketch of the scene in your journal and plan how you will use linear or aerial perspectives. Step 5: Share your sketch with your peers and teacher, and get their feedback. Step 6: Focus on linear perspective while making your finalised drawing. Step 7: Focus on aerial perspective when you colour your artwork. Step 8: Complete your artwork and display it in class. Step 9: Review the artworks done by others and make notes in your journal. Explore Mediums with Colour Theory
answer: Steps to create the perspective artwork: 1) Visualise dancers, postures and setting. 2) Make thumbnail sketches. 3) Mark horizon/eye level and vanishing point(s). 4) Use linear perspective for architecture and figure placement. 5) Apply aerial perspective in colour (muted, cooler distant colours). 6) Finalise, display, and record peer feedback.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 15.1 - Which Mediums Are You Interested In?
question: 1. Complementary colours are seen directly opposite to each other on the colour wheel. How many pairs of complementary colours can you list? Which combination do you like the most and why? Analogous colours lie next to each other on the colour wheel. Make a list of analogous colours in groups of three. Which combination do you like the most and why?
answer: Complementary pairs (examples): Red–Green; Blue–Orange; Yellow–Purple; Red-Orange–Blue-Green (tertiary complements). I like Blue–Orange for strong contrast and warmth/cool balance. Analogous groups of three: (Red, Red-Orange, Orange); (Blue, Blue-Green, Green); (Yellow, Yellow-Orange, Orange). Favourite analogous: Blue–Blue-Green–Green — calming and harmonious.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 15.1 - Which Mediums Are You Interested In?
question: 16. Visual Composition
answer: Visual composition: arranging visual elements (line, shape, colour, texture, space) using principles: balance, unity, rhythm, emphasis, proportion, and hierarchy to guide viewer attention and create coherent, expressive artworks.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 1. Activity 16.1. Activity 16.1 Create compositions: Choose one option from below and create a two-dimensional composition. Option A: Graphic story/ comic strip; Option B: Thematic painting; Option C: Collage. Option A: Create a four-part graphic story or comic strip - In this activity, you will create a comic strip with four parts or four scenes. It should have: 1. at least two characters created by you; 2. a setting: indoor, outdoor, or imaginary; and 3. continuity from one scene to another. Step 1. Ideation; Step 2. Choosing the size, format, and sequence; Step 3. Character sketches; Step 4. Speech balloons; Step 5. Composition of scenes; Step 6. Arrange the sequence: Select the iterations that work best and finalise the sequence of four scenes. Step 7. Refine: Finalise the drawings. Step 8. Colour: Use suitable colour combinations and contrast to colour each scene. Step 9. Display your completed artwork and review it among your peers. Option B: Thematic painting - In this activity, you will choose a theme for your composition and present it in the form of a coloured drawing, painting, or collage. Step 1: Select a medium based on the availability of materials and resources; Step 2: Decide the size of your artwork; Step 3: Choose a theme or topic; Step 4: Make iterations of your compositional layout; Step 5: Make a line drawing of the finalised composition; Step 6: Plan the colour scheme for your artwork based on the moods and emotions you would like to convey; Step 7: Colour your artwork in a planned sequence; Step 8: Add the final details and complete your work; Step 9: Think of three titles for your artwork and choose one after discussion; Step 10: Remember that title and topic are different; Step 11: Display your artwork in class and review it with your peers. Option C: Collage (Group work) - In this activity, you will work in groups and decide a theme collaboratively for your composition and present it in the form of a collage. Step 1: Choose your materials; Step 2: Decide the size of your artwork; Follow Steps 3 to 6 as given in Option B: Thematic Painting; Step 7: Experiment with the edges; Follow Steps 8 to 10 as given in Option B: Thematic Painting.
answer: Option A (comic strip): Create four scenes showing continuity, two original characters, simple dialogue balloons, thumbnails, final panels, and colour scheme. Option B (thematic painting): Choose theme, plan layout, line drawing, colour scheme for mood, finish details, suggest three titles. Option C (collage, group): Collect materials, agree theme, plan composition, experiment edges, assemble, refine and display.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
question: 17. Branches of Visual Arts
answer: Branches of Visual Arts: painting, drawing, sculpture, printmaking, photography, ceramics, textiles, graphic design, illustration, animation, film/video, architecture, craft, digital art, installation and performance-related visual practices.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 17.1 - Explore Branches of Visual Arts
question: 1. Activity 17.1. Activity 17.1: As you read about each category given below, choose one or two that interest you. Explore and document the work of any two artists, designers, or craftspersons mentioned. Refer to artists, view their artworks, and watch films/ interviews. Guiding questions: What kind of visual art does the artist practice? What had been their inspiration, and how did they learn the art form? What are the subjects or themes that they are interested in? Why do you think their work has received recognition? Note down your learnings and questions and present them in your class. Make notes from others' presentations as well. Activity 17.2 - Interact with Visual Art Professionals
answer: How to explore two artists: Choose two practitioners, note their art form, region, training, inspirations, materials and techniques, main themes, why they’re recognized, and sources (books, interviews, museum websites). Prepare images and 5–7 key points for class presentation.

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 17.1 - Explore Branches of Visual Arts
question: 1. Activity 17.2. Activity 17.2 Interact with visual art professionals: You may have many questions about branches of Visual Arts as well as visual artists. With the help of your teacher, find artists from your region, to contact and interact with, either in person or online to learn about the practical aspects of their work. Heritage Crafts
answer: How to interact with visual art professionals: With teacher help, contact local artists by phone/email; arrange in-person visits or video calls; prepare questions about training, daily routine, materials, pricing, markets, and tips for beginners; take notes and photos (with permission).

subject: Arts (Madhurima)
section: Activity 17.1 - Explore Branches of Visual Arts
question: 1. Find out about Padma awardees or any craftsperson from your region or state.
answer: How to find a Padma awardee or local craftsperson: Search the official Padma awards list (govt), local cultural centres, news articles, or ask elders. Record name, award/year, craft, region, notable works and contributions, and a source for verification.

subject: English
question: 1. Bharat Our Land Learning Beyond the Text
answer: Project intro: 'Bharat — Our Land' is an interdisciplinary project exploring India’s geographical diversity, cultures, languages, and how landscapes shape livelihoods and traditions. Plan research, field visits, maps, images, and presentations linking geography with everyday life.

subject: English
question: I–II. I Search for poems or songs dedicated to India, your motherland, in your regional language. Share them with your classmates and explain their meaning too. II In groups of six, prepare an interdisciplinary project on India’s major geographical features. For each feature, describe the region, explain its importance in the lives of the people living there and mention the languages spoken in that region. Include examples of mountains, rivers, deserts, valleys, islands, and plateaus. Listen and Respond
answer: I: Find regional patriotic poems/songs at libraries, family, or online; bring lines, translate meaning, and explain cultural context. II: Group project plan: divide features (mountains, rivers, deserts, valleys, islands, plateaus); for each, describe region, importance to people, languages spoken, examples (Himalayas, Ganga, Thar, Kashmir valley, Andaman, Deccan Plateau).

subject: English
question: I. You will listen to four people talk about the places they like to travel to. As you listen, write the speaker number for the two pictures given.
answer: Listening task (method): Without the audio we cannot assign speaker numbers. While listening, note distinct place-descriptions each speaker gives and mark the speaker number beside the matching picture. Use keywords (climate, activities, landmarks) to match accurately.

subject: English
question: II. You will once again listen to the four speakers. As you listen, match the given statements to the speaker. There are two statements you do not need. Speaking Activity
answer: Listening-match method: Cannot match statements without audio. Listen to each speaker again, note unique facts or opinions they state, then match statements that repeat those details. Two statements will remain unused; eliminate by checking for mismatch.

subject: English
question: I. In pairs, take turns to speak about the aspects of your village/town/city that you feel are an asset. It could be about geographical, cultural, traditional features, or even its history. (Use the given cues.) Writing Task
answer: Model 1-minute talk (example): My town’s river is an asset — it supplies water, supports fishing and festivals. Our old fort attracts tourists and local craftmakers sell handloom goods. People speak three languages; community events preserve traditional music and foods.

subject: English
question: I. Write a paragraph about a place that you have visited which has stayed in your memory. (Include reasons, companions, preparation, stay, activities.)
answer: Sample paragraph: I will always remember the hill-station trip with my cousins. We prepared by packing warm clothes and snacks. We stayed in a small guesthouse, trekked at dawn, and watched sunrise together. The clear air, laughter, and shared tea made it unforgettable.

subject: English
question: 1. How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
answer: Summary: 'How I Taught My Grandmother to Read' (Sudha Murty) is a touching true story about patience, literacy, family bonds and the joy of learning; it shows empathy, persistence and the social value of education.

subject: English
question: I. India has 22 major languages according to the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. Each language has its own unique identity. Talk to your classmates and teacher and complete the given table with words from any five Indian languages. Language     1. Kannada  2.   3.   4.   5. Grandmother   Avva Grandfather Mother Father Sister Brother
answer: Sample table with five Indian languages (fill by asking local speakers): 1. Kannada — Grandmother: Avva; Grandfather: Ajja; Mother: Amma; Father: Appa; Sister: Akka; Brother: Anna. 2. Hindi — दादी (Dadi); दादा (Dada); माँ (Maa); पिता/पापा (Pita/Papa); बहन (Behen); भाई (Bhai). 3. Tamil — பாட்டி (Paatti); தாத்தா (Thatha); அம்மா (Amma); அப்பா (Appa); அக்கா (Akka); அண்ணா (Anna). 4. Marathi — आजी (Aaji); आजोबा (Aajoba); आई (Aai); बाबा (Baba); बहीण (Bahīn); भाऊ (Bhau). 5. Bengali — দিদি/দিদা (Didi/Dida); দাদা (Dada); মা (Ma); বাবা (Baba); বোন (Bon); ভাই (Bhai). (Confirm spellings with speakers.)

subject: English
question: I. You will listen to a speaker talk about digital literacy. As you listen, complete the following sentences with one to three exact words that you hear.
answer: Listening blank 1 — method: Without the audio we cannot supply the exact words. While listening, write the exact one to three words the speaker uses; likely candidates: 'digital devices' or 'technology' or 'the internet'.

subject: English
question: 1. Literacy these days includes the ability to use _____________.
answer: Listening blank 2 — method: Cannot fill exactly without the audio. Listen for the phrase; likely answers: 'personal data', 'privacy', or 'our information'.

subject: English
question: 2. Digital literacy is also about protecting _____________.
answer: Listening blank 3 — method: Depends on audio. Probable phrasing: 'keep in touch', 'connect with family', or 'access services'. Write the exact words you hear (1–3 words).

subject: English
question: 3. Digital literacy enables the elderly to ______________.
answer: Listening blank 4 — method: Without audio we can’t be exact. Likely pair: 'scams and phishing' or 'fake information and scams'. Note the two exact words spoken in sequence.

subject: English
question: 4. Digital literacy encourages using the internet safely by helping us recognise ______________ and _______________.
answer: Listening blank 5 — method: Cannot provide the exact words here. Likely phrase: 'basic digital skills', 'digital training', or 'digital literacy'. Record the speaker’s exact 1–3 words when you listen.

subject: English
question: 5. The National Digital Literacy Mission helps people across the country by imparting ______________.
answer: The National Digital Literacy Mission helps people across the country by imparting basic digital literacy skills, such as using computers, internet, email, mobile apps, and safe online practices for education, banking, communication and government services.

subject: English
question: —. Turncoat is a type of solo debate where the speaker argues for and against a topic, switching sides after a certain period of time. I Choose your topic and speak ‘for’ and ‘against’ for not more than one minute each. Topic 1: It is important to learn a new language apart from your mother tongue. Topic 2: Learning can happen only when you are young. Use the guidelines given below. • Begin with speaking ‘for’ the topic for one minute. • Your teacher will signal that it is time to switch sides. • Then speak ‘against’ the topic for one minute. You may use the following sentence prompts. (‘For’ and ‘Against’ prompts as given.) Vocabulary and Structures in Context V (i). Fill in the blanks with simple past and past perfect tense form of the verbs given in brackets.
answer: Topic chosen: It is important to learn a new language apart from your mother tongue. FOR (≈1 min): Learning another language broadens horizons, improves communication, boosts career prospects, and strengthens cognitive skills. It fosters empathy and access to other cultures. AGAINST (≈1 min): Prioritising one’s mother tongue preserves identity; forcing another language can dilute cultural roots, overload students, and divert time from essential local knowledge and subjects.

subject: English
question: A. When the delegates _________ (arrive) at the conference, the keynote speaker _________ (already begin) the session.
answer: When the delegates arrived at the conference, the keynote speaker had already begun the session.

subject: English
question: B. After the students _________ (learn) how to identify fake news online, they _________ (start) verifying information before sharing it.
answer: After the students had learned how to identify fake news online, they started verifying information before sharing it.

subject: English
question: C. Before Kiran _________ (start) using digital payment platforms, she _________ (ensure) her understanding of online fraud prevention.
answer: Before Kiran started using digital payment platforms, she had ensured her understanding of online fraud prevention.

subject: English
question: D. By the time Varun _________ (recognise) the importance of budgeting, he _________ (exhaust) most of his savings.
answer: By the time Varun recognised the importance of budgeting, he had exhausted most of his savings.

subject: English
question: E. When Raghu _________ (log in) to the cybersecurity webinar, the instructor _________ (already discuss) the importance of strong passwords. V (ii). Fill in the blanks with the correct form of verbs given in brackets. Last year, my parents and I A. _________ (take) a financial planning course. When we B. _________ (review) our expenses, we realised we C. _________ (spend) too much on unnecessary purchases. After my parents D. _________ (discuss) ways to save, I E. _________ (open) a savings account. By the time we F. _________ (set) our budget, the course G. _________ (already introduce) investment strategies. We H. _________ (hurry) to take notes, but many participants I. _________ (complete) their financial plans. Despite that, we J. _________ (enjoy) learning how to manage money wisely.
answer: When Raghu logged in to the cybersecurity webinar, the instructor had already discussed the importance of strong passwords.

subject: English

subject: English

subject: English

subject: English
question: 9. work to bring out the imagined shape

question: —. TASK Make your own Meteorological Lab Build a simple meteorology observatory in your school with a (i) simple rain gauge, (ii) dry-wet bulb thermometer and (iii) wind vane. Follow the steps in Figures 1.3–1.5 using the materials suggested. You can always substitute the materials if you wish; please consult your teacher/an expert before doing so. Use your observatory to track rainfall, temperature (including the average and range of temperature) and wind direction. You should collect and analyse the data over three months, that is, the duration of the time you are doing this work. You can also create a weather bulletin board for farmers in your region. Section 1.3.1 – Soil testing and amendment Soil sample collection To carry out these tests, soil can be collected from your own garden or nearby fields. The process of sample collection is very important to get good results. Take soil from different spots, for example, from a sandy area, organic pit and water channel, and mix the samples, as soil quality can vary even within a small area. Avoid shady areas (like under trees) and places, where fertilisers are stored in the field. Remove stones, leaves and other debris. Dry the soil in sunlight for a few hours. Crush clumps and sieve the mixture to get fine soil suitable for testing. Label each sample carefully, for example, date of collection, whether the previous crop was grown, and use it for both mason jar texture tests and pH testing. Figure 1.6 will help you collect the soil samples. Testing soil for its clay and sand percentage (mason jar test) Understanding soil texture and pH is another crucial step in evaluating soil health. Soil texture is determined by the amount of sand (largest particles), silt (medium–sized particles) and clay (smallest particles). Soil texture affects how well the soil holds water, nutrients and how easily roots can grow in it. You can assess soil texture through a mason jar test. Figure 1.7 shows the process for the mason jar test. Section 1.3.2 – Seed selection Floating method
answer: Build simple instruments: Rain gauge — marked bottle; Wet-and-dry bulb — two thermometers, wet wick on one; Wind vane — arrow on pivot with compass. Record rainfall, temperature and wind direction daily for 3 months; prepare farmer bulletins. Soil sampling: collect mixed samples, dry, sieve, label. Mason jar test: mix soil+water, let settle, measure layers to compute sand/silt/clay percentages.

question: 1. Follow the pH testing process given in Chapter 1.

question: 3. Precision Farming Section 3.4.1 – Collecting weather data Collecting weather data and deciding which crop protection method to use. Section 3.8.4 – Deciding quantity of organic fertiliser Rough estimation of organic carbon in soil Take two soil samples in two small clear containers:
answer: Collect local weather data (school observatory, IMD, KVK) for rainfall, temperature and humidity; use Table 3.4 to choose protection (mulch, nets, biological controls). For organic carbon: prepare Samples A/B, add 3% H2O2, compare fizzing—more fizz = more OC.

subject: Kaushal Vikas
question: 1. Sample A (Control): Soil without addition of compost
answer: Sample A (control): soil without compost. After adding 3% H2O2 expect little or no bubbling, indicating lower organic carbon compared to enriched sample.

subject: Kaushal Vikas
question: 2. Sample B (Test): Soil enriched with compost. You will also need 3 per cent Hydrogen Peroxide (H2O2) Step 1: Prepare the Samples – Place small and equal amounts of debris-free soil samples A and B in two separate containers. Step 2: Add Hydrogen Peroxide – Pour hydrogen peroxide in both containers, such that both samples are saturated (wear safety gear during this step). Step 3: Observe the Reaction – Observe both samples for immediate fizzing, bubbling or foaming as hydrogen peroxide reacts with the Organic Carbon (OC) in the soil (an oxidation reaction), releasing oxygen gas (O2).
answer: Sample B (test): soil plus compost. Add 3% H2O2 while wearing safety gear; stronger fizzing/bubbling shows higher organic carbon. Record and compare intensity with Sample A.

question: 6. Construction Section 6.8.1 – Carrying out minor repair Carrying out minor repairs Step 1: Mix one part cement and three parts sand. Step 2: Add water slowly to make a smooth, thick paste. Step 3: Clean the surface and lightly sprinkle water on it. Then apply the mortar on cracks, joints, tiles or uneven surfaces using a trowel. Step 4: Press, level and smoothen the applied area.
answer: Mix cement:sand 1:3; add water slowly to make thick paste. Clean and dampen the surface. Apply mortar into cracks with a trowel. Press, level and smooth. Keep area moist to cure 24–48 hours. Wear gloves, mask and eye protection.

subject: Kaushal Vikas
question: 7. Apparel Section 7.10 – Sewing the product
answer: Sewing steps: prepare and align fabric pieces with seam allowance, pin, stitch seams (machine or hand), backstitch ends, trim and finish raw edges, attach fasteners (buttons/zippers), and press seams. Check fit and make adjustments as needed.

subject: Kaushal Vikas
question: —. PORTFOLIO Place a sketch or image of each step of the process in your portfolio. Briefly describe each step. Did you need to redo the stitching? If yes, why and what did you do differently the second time? Section 7.3 – Site visit You can use the pointers in Table 7.2 for discussion with practitioners and take notes. Section 7.4 – Technical drawing of apparel Think of different design options for the apparel you will make. Take measurements carefully. Make a neat technical drawing, detailing out the exact measurements and label all parts clearly. Also, write notes about fabric, thread or special features like zippers, buttons or embroidery. Section 7.5 – Selecting materials Which material did you select and why? Section 7.7 – Bill of Materials Prepare the Bill of Materials for the apparel you will make. Section 7.8.1 – Sewing Place the sampler or an image of the sampler in your portfolio. Practise different types of stitches on a sample cloth as shown in Figure 7.8. You can ask experts to teach you stitches other than those in Table 7.7 or search for videos on the Internet. You can also try to repair any apparel or stitch small covers for water glasses from recycled cloth for practice. Section 7.8.2 – Drafting Prepare a paper pattern of the apparel you will make using chart paper or old newspaper. Section 7.9 – Marking and cutting fabric Place images or sketches of each of the steps you took to prepare, mark and cut the fabric in your portfolio. Write a brief description of the step.
answer: Portfolio: place a sketch/photo for each step with a one-line description. If you redid stitching (e.g., puckering or loose tension), note cause and fix (adjust tension, change needle/thread, re-pin). For site visit ask tools/time/costs. Include technical drawing with measurements, BOM, sampler, paper pattern, and photos of marking and cutting.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
answer: Coordinates: draw perpendicular x- and y-axes with origin (0,0). An ordered pair (x,y) locates a point by moving x units horizontally from origin and y units vertically, then mark the point.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. What are the standard widths for a room door? Look around your home and in school.
answer: Common room-door widths: about 700–900 mm (approx. 2'4"–3'0"). Typical sizes include 750 mm, 800 mm and 900 mm; main or entrance doors may be 1000–1100 mm wide.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Are the doors in your school suitable for people in wheelchairs? Think and Reflect 2 (p. 27)
answer: Check if doors are ≥900 mm wide, have low thresholds, ramps, turning space and reachable handles. Many schools lack full accessibility; if yours meets these, they suit wheelchairs; otherwise add ramps, widen doors and adjust fittings.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. What is the x-coordinate of a point on the y-axis?
answer: The x-coordinate of any point on the y-axis is 0, because such points have zero horizontal distance from the origin.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Is there a similar generalisation for a point on the x-axis?
answer: Yes. Any point on the x-axis has y-coordinate 0, because such points have zero vertical distance from the origin.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 3. Does point Q ( y, x) ever coincide with point P ( x, y)? Justify your answer.
answer: P(x,y) and Q(y,x) coincide precisely when x = y. If x ≠ y the points are different, since ordered pairs are equal only when corresponding coordinates match.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 4. If x ≠ y, then ( x, y) ≠ (y, x); and ( x, y) = (y, x) if and only if x = y. Is this claim true? Think and Reflect 3 (p. 29)
answer: True. Ordered pairs are equal iff their coordinates match. If x ≠ y then (x,y) ≠ (y,x); and (x,y) = (y,x) holds exactly when x = y.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. In moving from A (3, 4) to D (7, 1), what distance has been covered along the x-axis? What about the distance along the y-axis?
answer: x-distance = 7 − 3 = 4 units to the right. y-distance = 1 − 4 = −3, so 3 units downward (magnitude 3).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Can these distances help you find the distance AD? Think and Reflect 4 (p. 31)
answer: Yes. Use Pythagoras: AD = √((Δx)^2+(Δy)^2) = √(4^2+(−3)^2) = √(16+9) = 5 units.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. What has remained the same and what has changed with this reflection?
answer: Reflection in the y-axis: y-coordinates and lengths stay the same; x-coordinates change sign. Shape and size unchanged, orientation becomes a left–right mirror image.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Would these observations be the same if ΔADM is reflected in the x-axis (instead of the y-axis)?
answer: Yes. For reflection in the x-axis: x-coordinates and lengths remain the same; y-coordinates change sign. Shape and size preserved, orientation becomes an up–down mirror image.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Introduction to Linear Polynomials
answer: Linear polynomial (one variable) has form ax + b with a ≠ 0. It is degree 1, has at most two terms, coefficient a for the variable and constant term b.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. Can you identify the terms, variables and coefficients of this algebraic expression?
answer: Identify terms (separated by +/−), variables (symbols like x,y) and coefficients (numbers multiplying variables). Example: 3x+5y−2 → terms: 3x, 5y, −2; variables: x,y; coefficients: 3 and 5.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. How is it different from the algebraic expression in Example 1? Think and Reflect 2 (p. 37)
answer: Compare degree, number of terms, variables and constants. A linear expression (degree 1) differs from higher-degree expressions by degree; differing constants or extra variables change form and graph.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Can you point out any similarity or difference between the algebraic expressions obtained in Examples 1 and 3?
answer: Look for similarities (same degree, same variables) and differences (different coefficients, extra or missing terms, different constant). These affect values and graphs but preserve algebraic rules.
