question: 3. The World of Numbers
answer: The World of Numbers: classification of numbers—natural, whole, integers, rational, irrational, real—with examples, inclusion relations and key properties used in arithmetic and algebra.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. Convert the following rational numbers in the form of a terminating decimal or non-terminating and repeating decimal, whichever the case may be, by the process of long division: (i) 3 50 (ii) 2 9
answer: (i) 3/50 = 0.06 (terminating). (ii) 2/9 = 0.222... (non-terminating, repeating digit 2). Obtain both by performing long division.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 10. A rational number has a terminating decimal expansion whose last non-zero digit occurs in the 4th decimal place. Show that such a number can be written in the form p 104 , where p is an integer not divisible by 10. Is it necessary that the denominator of this rational number, when written in the lowest form, is divisible by 2 4 or 5 4 ? Give reasons.
answer: If the last non-zero digit is at 4th decimal place, multiplying by 10^4 gives an integer p whose last digit is non-zero, so the number = p/10^4 with p not divisible by 10. Its reduced denominator q divides 2^4·5^4, so max(exponent of 2, exponent of 5)=4; hence q must be divisible by 2^4 or 5^4 (or both).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 11. Without performing division, determine whether the decimal expansion of 18 125 is terminating or non-terminating. If it terminates, state the number of decimal places.
answer: 125 = 5^3 divides 10^3, so 18/125 has a terminating decimal with at most 3 places. Multiply top and bottom by 8: 18/125 = 144/1000 = 0.144 (three decimal places).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 12. A rational number in its lowest form has denominator 2 3 × 5. How many decimal places will its decimal expansion have? Explain your answer.
answer: Denominator = 2^3×5 has exponents 3 and 1, so decimal expansion needs max(3,1)=3 places. The decimal terminates in 3 decimal places because denominator divides 10^3 but not 10^2.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 13. Let a = 7 12 and b = 5 6 . Express both a and b in the form k m 1 and k m 2 where k 1 , k 2 and m are integers and k 2 – k 1 > 6. Using the same denominator m, write exactly five distinct rational numbers lying between a and b keeping an integer numerator. Explain why the condition k 2 – k 1 > n + 1 is necessary to find n such rational numbers between the two rational numbers a and b using this method.
answer: Take m = 96 (12×8). Then a = 7/12 = 56/96 and b = 5/6 = 80/96, so k1=56, k2=80 and k2−k1=24>6. Five rationals between are 57/96, 58/96, 59/96, 60/96, 61/96. The condition k2−k1>n+1 ensures at least n integer numerators strictly between k1 and k2.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 14. Three rational numbers x, y, z satisfy x + y + z = 0 and xy + yz + zx = 0. Show that all the rational numbers x, y, z must be simultaneously zero.
answer: Square (x+y+z)=0: (x+y+z)^2 = x^2+y^2+z^2 +2(xy+yz+zx)=0. Given xy+yz+zx=0, we get x^2+y^2+z^2=0. Sum of squares is zero only if x=y=z=0 (for rationals).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 15. Show that the rational number ( a +b) 2 lies between the rational numbers a and b.
answer: Interpreting (a+b)/2: if a<b then a < (a+b)/2 < b. Proof: a < b ⇒ a < (a+b)/2 since (a+b)/2 − a = (b−a)/2>0, similarly (a+b)/2 < b. Thus (a+b)/2 lies between a and b.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 16. Find the lengths of the hypotenuses of all the right triangles in Fig. 3.14 which is referred to as the square root spiral.
answer: In the square-root (Theodorus) spiral successive hypotenuses are √2, √3, √4, √5, … . Each right triangle’s hypotenuse equals √n for n = 2,3,4,….

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Prove that 5 is an irrational number.
answer: Assume √5 = p/q in lowest terms. Then p^2 = 5q^2, so 5 divides p ⇒ p=5k. Then 25k^2 = 5q^2 ⇒ q^2 =5k^2, so 5 divides q, contradicting gcd(p,q)=1. Hence √5 is irrational.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 3. Convert the following decimal numbers in the form of p q . (i) 12.6 (ii) 0.0120 (iii) 3.052 (iv) 1.235 (v) 0.23 (vi) 2.05 (vii) 2.125 (viii) 3.125 (ix) 2.1625

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 4. Locate the following rational numbers on the number line. (i) 0.532 (ii) 1.15
answer: 0.532 = 532/1000 = 133/250 lies slightly after 0.53 (mark 0 and 1, divide 0–1 into 10, then refine hundredths/thousandths). 1.15 = 115/100 = 23/20 lies between 1.1 and 1.2, one-fifth of the way from 1.1 to 1.2.

question: 6. Find 5 rational numbers between 2 5 and 3 5 .
answer: Five rationals between 2/5 and 3/5: 11/25, 21/50, 23/50, 1/2, 12/25 (all between 0.4 and 0.6).

question: 7. Find 5 rational numbers between 1 6 and 2 5 .

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 9. Let a and b be two non-zero rational numbers such that a b + = 1 0 . Without assigning any numerical values, determine whether ab is positive or negative. Justify your answer. Exercise Set 3.5
answer: If a + b = 10 (a,b ≠ 0) the sign of ab cannot be determined: example positive ab: a=6,b=4 ⇒ ab=24; negative ab: a=11,b=−1 ⇒ ab=−11. So ab may be positive or negative.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Perform the long division for 1 13 . Identify the repeating block of digits. Does it show cyclic properties if you evaluate 2 13 ? Now compute 3 13 , 4 13 , etc. What do you notice?
answer: 1/13 = 0.076923 076923…; repeating block = 076923. 2/13,3/13,… give 153846,230769,… which are cyclic permutations of 076923 (multiples rotate the block).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 3. Classify the following numbers as rational or irrational: (i) 81 (ii) 12 (iii) 0.33333 … (iv) 0.123451234512345 … (v) 1.01001000100001 … (Notice the pattern: Is it repeating a single block?) (vi) 23.560185612239874790120 Find the explicit fractions in case they are rational.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 4. The number 0.9 (which means 0.99999 … ) is a rational number. Using algebra (let x = 0.9, multiply by 10, and subtract), explain why 0.9 is exactly equal to 1.
answer: Let x = 0.999… Then 10x = 9.999… Subtract: 9x = 9 ⇒ x = 1. Hence 0.999… = 1.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 5. We have seen that the repeating block of 1 7 is a cyclic number. Try to find more numbers ( n) whose reciprocals ( 1 n ) produce decimals with repeating blocks that are cyclic. Think and Reflect 1 (p. 69)
answer: More examples: 1/17, 1/19, 1/23, 1/29 often produce cyclic repeating blocks (length p−1 for suitable primes). Test by long division; if repetend length = p−1, multiples give cyclic permutations.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. While adding or subtracting two rational numbers having different denominators, how will you make the denominators equal?
answer: Make denominators equal by converting both fractions to a common denominator (preferably LCM of denominators). Multiply numerator and denominator of each fraction so both denominators equal, then add or subtract the numerators.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Verify the distributive law for rational numbers.
answer: Let x = a/b, y = c/d, z = e/f (rationals). x(y+z) = (a/b)((c/d)+(e/f)) = (a/b)((cf+de)/df) = acf/(bdf)+ade/(bdf) = xy + xz. Hence distributive law holds for rationals.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 4. Exploring Algebraic Identities
answer: Common algebraic identities: (a+b)^2 = a^2+2ab+b^2, (a-b)^2 = a^2-2ab+b^2, (a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2, a^3±b^3 = (a±b)(a^2∓ab+b^2). Verify by expanding both sides.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. Try to multiply the following using the distributive property. (x – y)(x 2 + xy + y 2 )
answer: (x–y)(x^2+xy+y^2) = x^3 + x^2y + xy^2 − x^2y − xy^2 − y^3 = x^3 − y^3. So it equals x^3 − y^3.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. (x + y)(x 2 – xy + y 2 ) Think and Reflect 1 (p. 91)
answer: (x+y)(x^2−xy+y^2) = x^3 − x^2y + xy^2 + x^2y − xy^2 + y^3 = x^3 + y^3. So it equals x^3 + y^3.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. What can you say about a and b if (a + b)2 < a2 + b2 ?
answer: Expand: (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2. If (a+b)^2 < a^2 + b^2 then 2ab < 0, so ab < 0. Thus a and b have opposite signs (one positive, one negative).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. What can you say about a and b if (a + b)2 > a2 + b2 ?
answer: If (a+b)^2 > a^2 + b^2 then 2ab > 0, so ab > 0. Thus a and b have the same sign (both positive or both negative).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 3. When will ( a + b)2 be equal to a2 + b2 ? Think and Reflect 2 (p. 98)
answer: (a+b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 when 2ab = 0, i.e. ab = 0. So the equality holds if at least one of a or b is zero.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. Try to evaluate the following using a suitable identity: (i) 352 (ii) 65 2 (iii) 85 2 (iv) 105 2 Do you observe any interesting pattern?
answer: Compute: 35^2=1225, 65^2=4225, 85^2=7225, 105^2=11025. Pattern: any number ending in 5: (10k+5)^2 = 100k(k+1)+25, so all squares end with 25 and leading part is k(k+1).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Observe the two rows of figures below. They represent an algebraic identity. Try to identify it. Think and Reflect 3 (p. 99)
answer: I can’t see the figures. To identify the identity: count shapes in each row, write each count as algebraic term (a^2, ab, b^2), equate rows. Common possibilities: (a+b)^2 = a^2+2ab+b^2 or a^3−b^3=(a−b)(a^2+ab+b^2).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 1. Figure out the product of x + 2 and x + 3 using algebra tiles.
answer: Using algebra tiles: (x+2)(x+3) gives one x^2 tile, five x-tiles, six unit tiles. So (x+2)(x+3) = x^2 + 5x + 6.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 2. Lay out algebra tiles for x2 + 11x + 30 in such a way that you will see its factors.
answer: Place one x^2 tile at a corner, put 6 x-tiles along one side and 5 x-tiles along the other, and fill the 5×6 interior with 30 unit tiles. This shows factors (x+5)(x+6).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
question: 5. I’m Up and Down, and Round and Round
answer: A point on the rim of a rolling circle traces a cycloid: x = r(t − sin t), y = r(1 − cos t). It goes up and down while the circle turns round and round.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 1. A, B and C are three collinear points. Can you find a point P such that PA = PB = PC ? What can you say about the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC? Draw and check. Can you show that for three collinear points A, B and C, the perpendicular bisector of AB and BC are parallel? Is it possible for a circle to pass through collinear points? Can you draw a line that cuts a given circle in three distinct points?
answer: No single point P (distinct) can satisfy PA = PB = PC for three distinct collinear A,B,C. Perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC are parallel (both perpendicular to line ABC). No circle can pass through three distinct collinear points; a line cannot cut a circle in three points.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 2. The circumcircle of a given ΔABC is drawn. Can there be other triangles congruent to ΔABC that share the same circumcircle? Think and Reflect 1 (p. 114)
answer: Yes. Rotate ΔABC about its circumcenter to get infinitely many congruent triangles on the same circumcircle; reflections across a diameter produce mirror-image congruent triangles as well.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 1. What are the rotational symmetries of a square? How many lines of reflection symmetry does it have? What about a regular pentagon? A regular hexagon?
answer: Square: rotations 0°,90°,180°,270° (4); reflection lines 4 (2 diagonals, 2 midlines). Regular pentagon: 5 rotations, 5 reflections. Regular hexagon: 6 rotations, 6 reflections (3 through opposite vertices, 3 through midpoints).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 2. What is the length of the longest chord in a circle of radius 5 units? Is there a smallest chord?
answer: Longest chord = diameter = 2×5 = 10 units. There is no smallest positive chord: chord lengths can be made arbitrarily small (approaching 0).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 3. The locus of points at a given distance from a given point is a circle. What can we say about the locus of points equidistant from two given points? (Hint: We know that any point that is equidistant from two given points A and B lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Does this make the perpendicular bisector the locus? For this, we have to show that all the points on the perpendicular bisector are equidistant from A and B.) Think and Reflect 2 (p. 115)
answer: The locus is the perpendicular bisector of AB. If P lies on it, let M be midpoint: triangles PAM and PBM are congruent (PM common, AM=BM, right angles), so PA=PB; hence every point on the bisector is equidistant from A and B.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 1. How many circles pass through two points on a plane?
answer: Infinitely many. Centers of all circles through two distinct points lie on their perpendicular bisector; choosing any center there (at suitable distance) gives a circle through the two points.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 2. Are there circles of all possible radii passing through A and B? What is the radius of the smallest circle passing through A and B? What is the radius of the largest circle passing through A and B?
answer: Not all radii are possible: radii must be ≥ AB/2. Smallest radius = AB/2 (center at midpoint). There is no largest radius; radii can be arbitrarily large as the center moves far away.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 3. As you move away from segment AB along its perpendicular bisector, do the radii of the circles containing A and B increase or decrease?
answer: They increase. If d is distance from the midpoint along the perpendicular bisector, radius r = sqrt((AB/2)^2 + d^2), so r grows as d increases.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 4. As you go along the perpendicular bisector, will the circle drawn from that point through A and B appear more curved or less curved?
answer: Less curved. As the centre moves along the perpendicular bisector away from AB, the radius through A and B grows, so curvature decreases and the circle looks flatter (less curved).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 5. You are given two points A and B on a plane. How many squares can you draw on the same plane with A and B on the boundary? How many squares can you draw on the plane with A and B as the corners of the square?
answer: Infinitely many squares with A and B merely on the boundary. With A and B as vertices there are three: two with AB as a side (one on each side) and one with AB as a diagonal.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 6. Measuring Space
answer: Measuring space: use standard units and tools — ruler/tape for lengths, unit squares or formulas for area, displacement or formulas for volume. Apply correct formula, measure carefully, and convert units as needed.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 19. Fig. 6.47: Nine identical rectangles stacked together The figure shows nine identical rectangles fitted together to make a large rectangle whose area is 72 cm 2 . Find the perimeter of each small rectangle.
answer: Each small rectangle has area 72/9 = 8 cm². Perimeter cannot be found from area alone; if sides are x and y with xy = 8, perimeter = 2(x + y). If square: side = 2√2 cm, perimeter = 8√2 cm.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 26. In Fig. 6.54, we see three triangles within a rectangle. The areas of the triangles are A, B, C, as marked. Show that the area of the rectangle is 2 A C B C C ( + ) ( + ) . Think and Reflect 1 (p. 154)
answer: Area of the rectangle = 2(A + B + C). Brief reason: the three marked triangles together occupy half the rectangle, so doubling their total area gives the whole rectangle's area.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 1. Think of various rectangles with perimeter 40 units (the sides do not have to be integers). How many such rectangles are there?
answer: Infinitely many. For perimeter 40, if one side is x then the other is 20 − x; any real x with 0 < x < 20 gives a rectangle with perimeter 40.

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 2. Among them, is there one whose area is the largest ? What are its dimensions?
answer: Yes — the square gives maximum area. For perimeter 40 the dimensions are 10 by 10, area 100 (from A = x(20 − x), maximized at x = 10 or by AM–GM).

subject: Mathematics (Ganita Manjari Part I)
section: Exercise Set 5.1 — Think, Draw and Infer (p. 118)
question: 3. Among all these rectangles, is there one whose area is the smallest? What are its dimensions? Do either of these answers come as a surprise to you?
answer: No smallest positive area. Area can be made arbitrarily small (approaching 0) as one side tends to 0 or 20; the degenerate case with a side 0 has area 0.

subject: Science
question: 1. Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
answer: Exploration method: observe phenomena, ask questions, review background, form a hypothesis, plan and do experiments, collect and record data, analyse results, draw conclusions and communicate findings.

subject: Science
question: 1. Think of a prediction you or your family made recently (for example, the outcome of a cricket match). Was it based on evidence and reasoning, or mainly on guesswork? How can scientific thinking improve such predictions? Example 1.2
answer: Example: we guessed a cricket result mainly by gut feeling. Scientific thinking would use evidence — past performance, pitch/weather, player fitness, and probabilities — giving better, testable, and more reliable predictions.

subject: Science
question: 1. Think of some questions Meghna could ask Varsha to make this prediction scientifically testable. Example 1.3
answer: Ask clear, measurable questions such as: What exactly do you predict will change? By how much and in what units? Which variable will you change (independent) and which will you measure (dependent)? What will be the control and how many trials?

subject: Science
question: 1. Estimate how many litres of air you breathe in one day. Start by estimating how many breaths you take per minute, and the volume of one breath. Your aim is not to find an exact answer, but a reasonable estimate. Pause and Ponder
answer: Estimate: breaths ≈ 15/min; tidal volume ≈ 0.5 L. Daily breaths = 15 × 60 × 24 = 21,600. Air per day ≈ 21,600 × 0.5 L = 10,800 L (≈10.8 m³).

subject: Science
question: 2. Cell: The Building Block of Life Activity 2.1: Let us estimate the size of a cell Activity 2.1. Activity 2.1: Let us estimate the size of a cell
answer: Method: measure microscope field diameter with a ruled scale, convert to μm, count cells across diameter, then size = field diameter (μm) ÷ number of cells. This gives an approximate cell size.

subject: Science
question: 1. Take a transparent ruler with millimetre (mm) markings.
answer: Take a transparent ruler marked in mm to place on the microscope stage; millimetre markings let you directly measure the diameter of the eyepiece field for later conversion to micrometres.

subject: Science
question: 2. Place the ruler on the stage of microscope, focus on it using the adjustment knob and observe the diameter of the circular field of view through the eyepiece and measure it in mm.
answer: Place the ruler on the stage, focus the microscope so the circular field is sharp, then read and record the diameter of the visible field in millimetres from the ruler.

subject: Science
question: 3. Convert the diameter from mm to micrometre (μm). Suppose the diameter of the visible field is 5 mm, meaning 5 × 1000 = 5000 μm.
answer: Convert mm to μm using 1 mm = 1000 μm. Example: if field diameter = 5 mm, then 5 × 1000 = 5000 μm.

subject: Science
question: 4. Remove the ruler and place an onion peel slide on the stage of the microscope.
answer: Prepare an onion peel slide: peel a thin translucent layer, place on a glass slide with a drop of water (or stain), cover with a coverslip, remove air bubbles, then place on the stage for observation.

subject: Science
question: 5. Focus on the slide and count the number of cells present along the diameter of the field of view in one straight line.
answer: Focus the onion slide, draw an imaginary straight line through the field centre, count cells along that diameter, and repeat counts in other fields for a reliable average.

subject: Science
question: 6. Estimate the real size of the cell using the formula: Estimated size of the onion peel cell = Diameter of the visible field in micrometre / Number of cells along the diameter Suppose, 25 cells are seen along the diameter. In that case, the size of one onion cell would be 5000 μm/25 = 200 μm. Activity 2.2: Let us experiment (potato osmosis) Activity 2.2. Activity 2.2: Let us experiment
answer: Use: cell size = field diameter (μm) ÷ number of cells. Example: 5000 μm ÷ 25 cells = 200 μm per onion cell. Activity 2.2 (potato osmosis) follows to test water movement.

subject: Science
question: 1. With the help of a kitchen knife, carefully cut a potato into two pieces of roughly equal size (Fig. 2.5).
answer: Carefully cut a potato into two equal pieces (similar shape/size). For osmosis: weigh pieces, place one in distilled water and one in salt solution for a few hours, then reweigh and record changes.

subject: Science
question: 2. Measure and record the initial weight of both the pieces using a weighing balance.
answer: Zero the digital balance, use clean weighing paper or dish, place each potato piece separately, record mass to nearest 0.01 g. Label readings as Sample A and Sample B and note time and room temperature.

subject: Science
question: 3. Put one piece of the potato in Beaker A with plain water.
answer: Use a clean beaker (50–100 mL), pour about 50 mL plain/distilled water, gently lower the first potato piece so it’s fully submerged, label the beaker 'A' and note the start time.

subject: Science
question: 4. Put the other piece of the potato in Beaker B with 20 per cent salt or sugar solution.
answer: Prepare 20% solution (20 g salt/sugar per 100 mL water; for 50 mL use 10 g). Pour into Beaker B, fully immerse the second potato piece, label 'B' and note the start time.

subject: Science
question: 5. Leave them undisturbed for about an hour or until you notice a visible change in the size of the pieces.
answer: Keep both beakers undisturbed at room temperature for about an hour. Place on a flat surface away from vibrations and direct sunlight. Check visually after 30 minutes and again at one hour, recording observations and times.

subject: Science
question: 6. Measure and record the final weight of each piece.
answer: Remove each piece carefully, blot excess liquid with tissue (do not squeeze), weigh on the same balance and dish as before, record final mass to the same precision and note the time measured.

subject: Science
question: 7. Calculate the difference between the initial and their final weights. What do you observe? You may observe that — Beaker A — The potato piece swells. Beaker B — The potato piece shrinks. What do you infer ? What do you expect in terms of changes in their weight? Activity 2.3: Let us investigate (onion and cheek cells) Activity 2.3. Activity 2.3: Let us investigate
answer: Calculate final minus initial mass for each piece. Expect Beaker A to gain weight (swells) as water enters by osmosis; Beaker B to lose weight (shrinks) as water exits into the hypertonic solution. Infer: water moves from low to high solute concentration across the cell membrane.

subject: Science
question: 1. Prepare temporary slides of a thin peel of an onion leaf or a Rhoeo (Cradle lily) leaf and mount it with safranin using cover slip to observe plant cells under a microscope.
answer: Peel a thin epidermis, place on a slide, add 1–2 drops safranin, lower a coverslip carefully, remove bubbles. Observe under 10x then 40x: rectangular cells with clear cell walls, stained cytoplasm and nucleus.

subject: Science
question: 2. Similarly, prepare a temporary slide of cheek cells by gently scraping the inner side of your cheek with a cotton swab or the blunt end of a toothpick.
answer: Rinse mouth, gently scrape inner cheek with a sterile cotton swab or blunt toothpick, avoid gagging. Use the swab immediately to transfer cells onto a slide; dispose the swab safely afterwards.

subject: Science
question: 3. Spread the cheek cells on a clean glass slide.
answer: Roll the swab across a clean slide to spread cheek cells in a thin smear, add a drop of water to loosen cells if needed, air dry briefly before staining or fixing.

subject: Science
question: 4. Add a drop of water followed by a few drops of methylene blue stain and carefully place a coverslip.
answer: Place one drop of water on the smear, add 1–2 drops methylene blue, lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid bubbles, blot excess stain. Under microscope nuclei and cell membranes will appear clearly stained.

subject: Science
question: 5. Observe both the slides under a microscope. What do you observe? Onion peel cells or Rhoeo leaf peel cells are box-shaped and regularly arranged, whereas cheek cells are irregularly arranged. Why do you think this difference exists? Prepare two slides of a Rhoeo leaf peel and human cheek cells again, and put 20 per cent sugar solution on them. Observe them under a microscope after half an hour. What do you observe? Activity 2.4: Let us study Activity 2.4. Activity 2.4: Let us study
answer: Observe: Rhoeo/onion peel cells are box-shaped, regularly arranged (rigid cell wall); cheek cells are irregular and loosely arranged (no cell wall). In 20% sugar (hypertonic): plant cells plasmolyse (membrane pulls from wall); cheek cells shrink and appear wrinkled.

subject: Science
question: 1. Study the given diagrams of a bacterial cell, a plant cell, and an animal cell (Fig. 2.10a, b and c).
answer: Bacterial cell: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid (no true nucleus), ribosomes, sometimes flagella/plasmids. Plant cell: cell wall, cell membrane, large central vacuole, chloroplasts, nucleus, mitochondria. Animal cell: cell membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, lysosomes, small vacuoles.

subject: Science
question: 2. Observe the different structures present in each of them.
answer: Observe differences: bacteria lack a true nucleus; plants and bacteria have cell walls (different composition); only plants have chloroplasts and large central vacuole; animals have lysosomes and centrioles; shapes differ (plant regular, animal variable).

subject: Science
question: 3. Record your observations in Table 2.1. Activity 2.5: Let us enhance our skills (onion root tip mitosis) Activity 2.5. Activity 2.5: Let us enhance our skills
answer: For Table 2.1 record: cell type, presence/absence of cell wall, nucleus, chloroplasts, vacuole size, typical shape, special structures and examples. For onion-root mitosis list observed stages (interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase), counts and small labeled sketches.

subject: Science
question: 1. Take a jar and fill it up with plain water.
answer: Use a clean jar and fill with plain water to a level that will reach the base (basal plate) of the bulb but not submerge the whole bulb; clean water ensures healthy root growth.

subject: Science
question: 2. Now, place an onion bulb over the jar in such a way that its base bearing roots, is immersed in the water.
answer: Place the onion bulb so its base (bearing root initials) just touches the water; support it with foil, a bottle top or cotton so only the basal plate is immersed and the bulb crown stays dry.

subject: Science
question: 3. Leave the setup for 5–6 days and observe. Do you observe the roots growing? Cut 2–3 cm of the freshly grown roots and transfer them to freshly prepared aceto-alcohol (glacial acetic acid:ethanol :: 1:3). Keep the root tips in aceto-alcohol for 24 hours and then transfer them to 70 per cent ethanol (for preservation).
answer: After 5–6 days roots appear. Cut 2–3 cm of fresh root tips and fix them in aceto-alcohol (glacial acetic acid:ethanol :: 1:3) for 24 hours, then transfer to 70% ethanol for preservation (use gloves and teacher supervision).

subject: Science
question: 4. Take one or two preserved roots, wash them in water and then, place them on a clean slide.
answer: Wash preserved root tips in water to remove fixative, blot gently, place 1–2 tips on a clean slide with their ends aligned toward the coverslip; add a drop of water to keep them moist.

subject: Science
question: 5. Put one drop of dilute Hydrochloric acid (HCl) on the root tips to soften the tissue. Rinse the roots after 10–15 minutes. Then add 2–3 drops of aceto-carmine stain on them.
answer: Add one drop dilute HCl on root tips for 10–15 minutes to soften tissue, then rinse. Place 2–3 drops aceto-carmine stain on the roots to stain chromosomes; wait 5–10 minutes. Handle acids and stains with care under supervision.

subject: Science
question: 6. Leave the slide for 5–10 minutes and then, gently warm it (with caution) over a spirit lamp.
answer: After staining, gently warm the slide (briefly over a spirit lamp) to intensify staining—do not overheat. Then place a coverslip and perform a gentle squash to spread cells; observe under microscope to identify mitotic stages.

subject: Science
question: 7. Cut the tip portion of the root on the slide and put a coverslip. Gently squash the coverslip with your thumb to spread the cells on the slide.
answer: Gently squashing spreads cells into a thin single layer so individual cells separate for viewing; this reveals cell walls, nuclei and mitotic stages. Use light pressure to avoid bursting cells or cracking the coverslip.

subject: Science
question: 8. Observe the slide under a microscope. What do you observe? Do you observe the cells of the onion root tip? Are they similar in structure? Do you find any structural differences in these cells? If yes, why is it so? Think It Over
answer: You will see many rectangular onion cells; most look similar but some differ—some show clear nuclei, others condensed chromosomes or mitotic figures. Differences arise because cells are in different stages of the cell cycle or are differentiating.

subject: Science
question: 1. Where does a cell come from?
answer: A cell comes from a pre-existing cell by cell division: body cells arise by mitosis, and reproductive cells (gametes) are produced by meiosis.

subject: Science
question: 2. How have technological interventions facilitated the creation of new knowledge in understanding the world beyond the naked eye?
answer: Microscopes (light, electron), stains, microtomes and digital imaging let us see tiny structures and processes beyond the naked eye, revealing organelles, microbes and cellular events and creating new biological knowledge.

subject: Science
question: 3. How is the cell structural and functional unit of life?
answer: A cell is the structural and functional unit of life because it builds tissues and organs and performs life processes (nutrition, respiration, growth, reproduction); unicellular organisms carry out all functions within one cell.

subject: Science
question: 4. How does a cell multiply?
answer: A cell multiplies by cell division: mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells for growth and repair; meiosis produces genetically varied gametes for sexual reproduction.

subject: Science
question: 3. Tissues in Action Activity 3.1: Let us design experiments (onion root growth jars) Activity 3.1. Activity 3.1: Let us design experiments
answer: Design: use two jars—control and treatment (e.g., different light or salt). Keep bulb type, temperature and water equal. Measure root length daily for 7 days, photograph and record averages; repeat for reliability.

subject: Science
question: 1. Take two glass jars or couplin jars and fill them with water.
answer: Fill each jar with water so the bulb’s basal plate just touches the water (about 1–2 cm). Label jars and avoid overfilling to prevent bulb rot.

subject: Science
question: 2. Now, take two onion bulbs and place one in each jar, as shown in Fig. 3.1.
answer: Place one onion bulb in each jar with the basal plate down so roots can grow into the water; support bulbs with mesh, foil or a ring if they float. Label jars.

subject: Science
question: 3. Observe the growth of roots in both bulbs for a few days.
answer: Observe daily for several days: measure root length with a ruler, count roots, note color/health and take photos. Record data in a table to compare growth between the two bulbs.

subject: Science
question: 4. Measure the length of roots on days 1, 2 and 3.
answer: Use a ruler to measure each root from the base of the onion bulb to its tip on days 1, 2 and 3. Record lengths in cm (to nearest mm) in a table: Day 1, Day 2, Day 3.

subject: Science
question: 5. On day 3, cut the root tips of the onion bulb in Jar B by about 1 cm. After this, observe the growth of roots in both the jars, measure their lengths for four more days (day 4 onwards), and record your observations in Table 3.1. What trend do you observe in the data you recorded in Table 3.1? Are your observations similar to those presented in the graphical representation (Fig. 3.2)? What do you infer? Activity 3.2: Let us understand further Activity 3.2. Activity 3.2: Let us understand further y Recall everyday experiences given in the first column of Table 3.3. y Write your observations and questions in your notebook. y Compare your observations with the observations given in Table 3.3. Table 3.3: Your experiences, observations and questions from daily life Experiences — Observations — Questions When you get a small cut on your skin — Red blood oozes out from the cut. A clot is formed after some time. — What causes blood to clot? When you get a skin infection — The area turns red and perhaps slightly swollen. You may have a fever. — (student to write) When you exercise or run — You breathe faster. Your face may turn red. — (student to write) The everyday experiences mentioned above are related to blood and its components.
answer: After cutting Jar B root tips on day 3, measure roots daily for days 4–7. Typical trend: Jar A shows steady growth; Jar B shows slowed or reduced growth immediately after cutting, then slower regrowth. This matches graphs showing root-tip damage reduces growth, so root tips (meristem) are essential for elongation.

subject: Science
question: 1. The red colour of blood is due to haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein in the Red Blood Cells (RBCs). RBCs live for about 4 months and are replaced regularly.
answer: True. Haemoglobin, an iron-containing protein in RBCs, gives blood its red colour. Red blood cells live about four months (≈120 days) and are constantly replaced by new cells produced in bone marrow.

subject: Science
question: 2. Platelets help in blood clotting at the site of the injury.
answer: True. Platelets help blood clotting by sticking to the wound, forming a temporary plug, and promoting fibrin formation to stabilise the clot and stop bleeding.

subject: Science
question: 3. During exercise or running, muscles need more oxygen, so breathing becomes faster and blood flow increases (face appears red).
answer: During exercise muscles need more oxygen and nutrients, so breathing rate and heartbeat increase, and more blood flows to muscles. This increased blood flow can make the face appear red.

subject: Science
question: 4. White Blood Cells (WBCs) collect at infected areas, causing pus formation and inflammation (causing redness and swelling, and possible pus formation at the infected area). Activity 3.3: Let us perform (identify connective tissues) Activity 3.3. Activity 3.3: Let us perform
answer: At infection sites WBCs migrate to destroy microbes; their activity and dead cells form pus. WBC response also causes inflammation — redness, swelling, pain — as part of the immune reaction.

subject: Science
question: 1. Perform the actions given in Table 3.4.
answer: Carry out actions (e.g., bend joints, pull skin, move fingers) and note feel and movement. Identify connective tissues: bone (hard support), cartilage (flexible support), tendon (muscle-to-bone), ligament (bone-to-bone), adipose (fat), blood (fluid connective tissue).

subject: Science
question: 2. Record your experiences and compare them with the experiences given in Table 3.4.
answer: Make a three-column record: Action — Observation — Identified connective tissue/function. Example: 'Bend knee — smooth joint movement — cartilage; pull skin — elastic return — areolar tissue.' Compare each entry with Table 3.4 and note similarities/differences.

subject: Science
question: 3. Study their functions and identify the connective tissues (Fig. 3.12). Activity 3.4: Let us investigate (body weight components) Activity 3.4. Activity 3.4: Let us investigate What percentage of total body weight comes from bones and muscles?
answer: Connective tissues and functions: Bone — support and protection; Cartilage — flexible support, cushioning; Tendons — attach muscle to bone; Ligaments — join bones at joints; Adipose — fat storage, insulation; Blood — transport of gases and nutrients.

subject: Science
question: 1. Step on a weighing scale and record your total body weight.
answer: Stand on a calibrated weighing scale, ensure zero before stepping on, stand still and read weight in kg to one decimal place. Record this value as your total body weight.

subject: Science
question: 2. Use online references or health resources to find average bone and muscle mass percentage for your age, gender, and an Indian body type (these may vary by ethnicity). For example, on average, adult males have about 40 – 50 per cent muscle, and adult females have ~30 – 40 per cent muscle, although bone mass is about 12 – 15 per cent for all adults.
answer: Typical average ranges: adult males ~40–50% muscle, adult females ~30–40% muscle. Bone mass for adults ≈12–15%. For Indian body types ranges are similar; check local sources (National Institute of Nutrition, WHO) for age/gender-specific values.

subject: Science
question: 3. Multiply your total body weight by the bone percentage and muscle percentage to estimate the weight of your bones and muscles.
answer: Method: muscle weight = body weight × muscle%. Bone weight = body weight × bone%. Example: 50 kg body; muscle 45% → 50×0.45 = 22.5 kg; bone 13% → 50×0.13 = 6.5 kg.

subject: Science
question: 4. Record the estimated bone weight and muscle weight, and compare them with your total body weight.
answer: Record example: bones 6.5 kg, muscles 22.5 kg (total 50 kg). Compare: bones+muscles < total because organs, fat, water and other tissues make up the remainder of body mass.

subject: Science
question: 5. Compare your findings with those of your classmates and calculate the class average. Discuss why bone and muscle mass differ between individuals, and how do they contribute to the overall body weight?
answer: Class average: sum all students' bone weights ÷ number of students; same for muscle. Differences arise from age, sex, genetics, activity, nutrition and hormones. Bones and muscles are substantial contributors to body weight; muscle is denser than fat.

subject: Science
question: 4. Describing Motion Around Us Activity 4.1: Let us analyse Activity 4.1. Activity 4.1: Let us analyse
answer: Activity 4.1 analysis: the ball moves vertically along one straight line (up and back down). Use distance (total path length travelled) and displacement (straight-line change from O, signed) to describe its motion.

subject: Science
question: 1. As shown in Fig. 4.5, a ball is thrown vertically upwards from O. It moves up straight till B and then falls back to O. Can this be considered a motion in a straight line?
answer: Yes. The motion is along a straight vertical line (same path), although direction changes at the top — still straight-line motion but with reversal.

subject: Science
question: 2. For this motion, fill up the values in Table 4.1. Table 4.1: Distance travelled and displacement of the ball
answer: How to fill Table 4.1: for a point at height h while going up: distance = h, displacement = +h. While coming down to height h: distance = h_peak + (h_peak − h), displacement = +h (if above O) or negative if below O.

subject: Science
question: S. No. Position — Total distance travelled by the ball from O till that position — Displacement of the ball from O till that position
answer: Interpretation: 'Total distance travelled' = length of path from O to that position following motion. 'Displacement' = straight-line distance from O to that position, with sign (+ upward, − downward) and units in cm.

subject: Science
question: 1. O — 0 cm — 0 cm
answer: O — Total distance traveled: 0 cm — Displacement from O: 0 cm.

subject: Science
question: 2. A — 40 cm — 40 cm in upward direction
answer: A — Total distance traveled: 40 cm — Displacement from O: +40 cm (upward).

subject: Science
question: 3. B —
answer: Answer: B.

subject: Science
question: 4. C —
answer: Answer: C.

subject: Science
question: 5. O —
answer: Answer: O.

subject: Science
question: 3. Analyse the data filled in Table 4.1 and choose which of the following is true for displacement: (i) It is never zero. (ii) Its magnitude can be greater than the total distance travelled. (iii) Its magnitude is less than or equal to the total distance travelled. (iv) Its magnitude is less than the total distance travelled in all cases. Activity 4.2: Let us calculate Activity 4.2. Activity 4.2: Let us calculate
answer: (iii) Its magnitude is less than or equal to the total distance travelled; it equals distance for unidirectional motion and is ≤ distance always.

subject: Science
question: 1. The magnitude of average acceleration of cars is generally specified as the time taken by the car to go from 0 km h–1 to 100 km h–1. Look it up on the internet and find this time for various cars, and record those in Table 4.2.
answer: Method and sample entries: convert 0→100 km/h = 27.78 m/s. Record times from internet. Example: Hatchback — 9 s; Sedan — 8 s; Sports car — 4 s. Fill Table 4.2 with those times.

subject: Science
question: 2. Calculate the magnitude of average acceleration for each car. Table 4.2: The magnitude of average acceleration in a time interval Car type — Time interval during which the speed goes from 0 to 100 km h–1 — Magnitude of average acceleration (m s–2) Activity 4.3: Let us plot a graph Activity 4.3. Activity 4.3: Let us plot a graph
answer: Compute aavg = Δv/Δt with Δv = 27.78 m/s (0→100 km/h). Example: 9 s → 3.09 m/s²; 8 s → 3.47 m/s²; 4 s → 6.95 m/s². Fill values in Table 4.2.

subject: Science
question: 1. Take a sheet of graph paper. This paper is pre-divided into small squares (Fig. 4.11a), making it easier to plot data accurately.
answer: Use graph paper with small squares. Title the graph, draw axes, label units, choose scale to use most paper, mark origin O clearly, and draw plotted points accurately on intersections.

subject: Science
question: 2. On the graph paper, draw two lines perpendicular to each other as shown in Fig. 4.11a. Their point of intersection is known as origin O. Mark the horizontal line as OX. It is known as the X-axis. Similarly, mark the vertical line as OY. It is called the Y-axis.
answer: Draw two perpendicular lines intersecting at O. Label horizontal OX as X-axis and vertical OY as Y-axis. Add arrowheads, units, and evenly spaced tick marks from the origin.

subject: Science
question: 3. Refer to Table 4.3. We need to decide which quantity (time or position) to be shown along each axis. For the data we have (Table 4.3), we will show time along the X-axis and position along the Y-axis.
answer: Plot time on the X-axis and position on the Y-axis because time is the independent variable and position depends on time.

subject: Science
question: 4. Determine a suitable scale for each quantity to represent it on the graph paper. We need to choose scales that allow us to represent the data effectively and conveniently while utilising the available space. The scale can be X-axis: 5 divisions = 1 s; Y-axis: 5 divisions = 20 m.
answer: Choose convenient scales to fit data: example X-axis 5 divisions = 1 s; Y-axis 5 divisions = 20 m. Ensure scales use available paper and evenly represent the range of values.

subject: Science
question: 5. Use the chosen scale to mark values for time (1 s, 2 s, …) along the X-axis from the origin. Similarly, mark values for position (20 m, 40 m, …) along the Y-axis (Fig. 4.11b).
answer: Choose scales so the graph fits the paper. Example: X-axis 1 s = 1 cm (label 0–6 s), Y-axis 20 m = 1 cm (label 0–120 m). Mark equal ticks from the origin and write the numeric values.

subject: Science
question: 6. Begin plotting points on the graph paper to represent each set of time and position values from Table 4.3.
answer: For each (t, s) from Table 4.3, find t on the X-axis and s on the Y-axis; place a small dot at their intersection. Use a sharp pencil and ruler for accuracy; label points if needed (A, B, C...).

subject: Science
question: 7. Once all points are plotted, connect them to create the position-time graph for the vehicle’s motion (Fig. 4.11c). It is a straight line for the data given in Table 4.3. Activity 4.4: Let us calculate (velocity from position-time graph) Activity 4.4. Activity 4.4: Let us calculate
answer: Use a ruler to join the plotted points. If they lie on a straight line, draw a single straight line—this indicates uniform motion. If points scatter slightly, draw a best-fit straight line through the set.

subject: Science
question: 1. In the position-time graph we plotted (Fig. 4.11c), consider a part (say, AB) of the graph as shown in Fig. 4.14. From A, draw a line parallel to X-axis and another line parallel to Y-axis. Repeat the same from B.
answer: From point A draw a horizontal line (parallel to X) and a vertical line (parallel to Y); repeat for B. Their intersections give coordinates t1, s1 and t2, s2, forming triangle ABC used to compute slope (velocity).

subject: Science
question: 2. Extend the horizontal line from A and a triangle ABC is formed. What do the sides BC and CA of the triangle represent? BC represents the change in position (s2 − s1), and AC represents the change in time (t2 − t1).
answer: BC represents the change in position, s2 − s1. CA represents the change in time, t2 − t1.

subject: Science
question: 3. As per Eq. (4.2a), by dividing the change in position (BC) by the change in time (CA), you get the average velocity v = (s2 − s1)/(t2 − t1).
answer: Average velocity v = (change in position)/(change in time) = BC/CA = (s2 − s1)/(t2 − t1).

subject: Science
question: 4. By extracting values of time t1 and t2, and distances s1 and s2 from the graph, the magnitude of average velocity can be calculated.
answer: Read coordinates (t1, s1) and (t2, s2) from the graph, compute s2 − s1 and t2 − t1, then divide to get the magnitude of average velocity. Include units (m/s).

subject: Science
question: 5. Exploring Mixtures and their Separation Activity 5.1: Let us experiment — Group activity Activity 5.1. Activity 5.1: Let us experiment — Group activity Divide the class into three groups — A, B and C. Each group prepares a mixture in a colourless, transparent glass tumbler or a 100 mL beaker by following these steps:
answer: Divide the class into Groups A, B, C. Each group prepares a mixture in a clear tumbler or 100 mL beaker as instructed, records observations (appearance, solubility), and later tests suitable separation methods.

subject: Science
question: 1. Group A: Add one spatula of common salt to 50 mL of water in a beaker and stir it well. Label it A.
answer: Group A: Add one spatula of common salt to 50 mL water and stir. Observation: salt dissolves to form a clear homogeneous solution. Label the container 'A' and note solubility and appearance.

subject: Science
question: 2. Group B: Add one spatula of chalk powder to 50 mL of water in a beaker and stir it well. Label it B.
answer: Group B: Add one spatula of chalk powder to 50 mL water and stir. Observation: suspension forms—water becomes cloudy, particles do not dissolve and may settle; heterogeneous mixture separable by filtration. Label the container 'B'.

subject: Science
question: 3. Group C: Add a few drops of milk to 50 mL of water in a beaker and stir it well. Label it C.
answer: Mixture C: Add a few drops of milk to 50 mL water, stir until uniformly cloudy. Label the beaker ‘C’. Appearance: milky, opaque—milk forms fine dispersed droplets (a colloid) in water.

subject: Science
question: 4. Are the particles visible in each mixture? Record your observations.
answer: Observations: Suspensions (e.g., sand in water) show visible particles; true solutions (salt/sugar) show no visible particles; milk (colloid) looks cloudy but individual particles are not seen with the naked eye.

subject: Science
question: 5. Direct the light from a laser pointer through the beakers containing the mixtures (Fig. 5.3) and observe it from the side of the beaker in a direction perpendicular to the laser beam. Safety first: Do not look directly into the laser beam. It can cause irreversible eye damage.
answer: Laser test: A visible beam (Tyndall effect) appears through the milk (colloid) and through suspensions because particles scatter light; no visible beam in a true solution. Safety: never look into the laser.

subject: Science
question: 6. Predict what you would observe in each of the beakers if you leave them undisturbed for a few minutes.
answer: Predictions: Suspensions will settle with particles forming sediment at the bottom; true solutions remain clear and unchanged; colloids like milk will remain evenly dispersed and cloudy for several minutes without rapid settling.

subject: Science
question: 7. Set up a filtration apparatus and filter each mixture separately. Is there any residue left on the filter paper?
answer: Filtration: Suspensions leave residue on the filter paper; true solutions pass through with no residue; colloids (milk) may partially pass, clog the paper, or leave some residue depending on pore size.

subject: Science
question: 8. Based on your observations, do you think these are the same types of mixtures or are they different? Activity 5.3: Let us prepare (crystals) Activity 5.3. Activity 5.3: Let us prepare
answer: Conclusion: They are different mixtures — suspension (particles settle), true solution (homogeneous, no visible particles), and colloid (cloudy, shows Tyndall effect, does not easily settle).

subject: Science
question: 1. Collect a sample of copper sulfate (blue vitriol). If copper sulfate is unavailable, you can use common salt as an alternative. Safety first: Copper sulfate is toxic. Perform the experiment under adult supervision and do not touch it with your bare hands.
answer: Collect copper sulfate (or use common salt as a safer alternative). Handle copper sulfate under adult supervision, wear gloves, avoid skin contact, and do not inhale or ingest the chemical.

subject: Science
question: 2. Take 1 g of copper sulfate and place it in a 100 mL beaker. Add 25 mL of water to the beaker and add a drop of dilute sulfuric acid. Gently heat the mixture in a water bath while stirring constantly. Sulfuric acid helps in making pure crystals by preventing unwanted reactions. Safety first: It is advised that the teacher should add a drop of sulfuric acid. Handle sulfuric acid very carefully!
answer: Method: Place 1 g CuSO4 in a 100 mL beaker, add 25 mL water, then one drop of dilute H2SO4 (teacher adds). Heat gently in a water bath while stirring until dissolved; use safety gear.

subject: Science
question: 3. Gradually, add more copper sulfate until the solution becomes saturated (Fig. 5.8a).
answer: Saturation step: Gradually add more copper sulfate while heating and stirring. Stop when added crystals no longer dissolve and undissolved solid remains—this indicates the solution is saturated.

subject: Science
question: 4. Filter the hot solution to remove insoluble impurities (Fig. 5.8b). Collect it in a clean beaker and cover it with a watch glass.
answer: Filtration and crystallization: Filter the hot solution with folded filter paper into a clean beaker to remove insolubles. Cover the beaker with a watch glass and let it cool undisturbed for crystals to form.

subject: Science
question: 5. Allow the solution to cool slowly without disturbing it (Fig. 5.8c). It gives enough time to the particles in the solution to come together, resulting in the formation of larger, shiny, well-shaped and blue-coloured crystals.
answer: Slow cooling reduces nucleation and gives particles time to join an existing lattice, forming fewer, larger, shiny, well-shaped blue crystals with orderly arrangement.

subject: Science
question: 6. Filter the crystals, rinse them with cold water and allow them to dry on a watch glass (Fig. 5.8d). Activity 5.5: Let us investigate (paper chromatography) Activity 5.5. Activity 5.5: Let us investigate
answer: Rinse removes adhering mother liquor and impurities; drying on a watch glass yields pure crystals. Activity 5.5: use paper chromatography to separate ink dyes by solvent rising through paper.

subject: Science
question: 1. Take a 3 cm wide strip of chromatographic paper and draw a straight, horizontal line, 2 cm from the bottom of the paper with a pencil (Fig. 5.15a). Alternatively, you can use a strip of filter paper.
answer: Use a 3 cm wide strip of chromatography or filter paper. Draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom as the baseline—pencil won’t dissolve or interfere with separation.

subject: Science
question: 2. Mark a spot with a black sketch pen at the centre of the line (Fig. 5.15b).
answer: Make a small black-ink dot at the centre of the pencil line and let it dry; this is the sample spot from which components will separate.

subject: Science
question: 3. Take enough water to make a thin layer at the bottom of a gas jar, a measuring cylinder, or a beaker.
answer: Pour a thin layer of solvent (water or chosen solvent) into the container, keeping the liquid level below the baseline so the spot is not submerged.

subject: Science
question: 4. Place the paper strip with the ink spot vertically into the container, so that its lower end dips into the water. The water level should be below the spot, as shown in Fig. 5.15c.
answer: Place the paper strip vertically with its lower end in the solvent and the ink spot above the solvent level; capillary action will draw solvent up the paper.

subject: Science
question: 5. Observe the paper as the water rises through the paper. What do you notice?
answer: You will observe the solvent front rising and the ink spot moving and splitting into separate coloured spots that travel different distances up the paper.

subject: Science
question: 6. As the water rises, the ink starts to separate into different colour spots. What can you infer from this? Safety note: solvent choice and safety cautions included in source. Activity 5.6: Let us separate (separating funnel) Activity 5.6. Activity 5.6: Let us separate
answer: Inference: the black ink is a mixture of different dyes. Components separate because they differ in solubility and affinity for the paper (stationary phase) and solvent (mobile phase).

subject: Science
question: 1. Pour a mixture of 5 mL mustard oil and 20 mL water into a 50 mL separating funnel.
answer: Pouring the mixture produces two immiscible layers: mustard oil and water separate because they do not mix, with oil forming the upper layer.

subject: Science
question: 2. Let it stand undisturbed. What do you observe?
answer: After standing undisturbed, you observe two distinct layers with a clear interface: oil remains on top and water settles below due to density and immiscibility differences.

subject: Science
question: 3. You will see the formation of two separate layers of mustard oil and water (Fig. 5.16). The yellow-coloured mustard oil forms the upper layer and water forms the lower layer. Can you explain why?
answer: Mustard oil floats above water because the two liquids are immiscible (different polarity) and oil is less dense than water, so it forms the upper layer.

subject: Science
question: 4. Open the stopcock of the separating funnel slowly to collect the lower layer of water carefully into a container.
answer: Place a clean container under the stopcock, open it very slowly so only the lower water layer flows out, and replace the container when nearly full to avoid spills.

subject: Science
question: 5. Close the stopcock when the water is almost fully drained.
answer: Close the stopcock when the water level is just above the tap to stop flow; this prevents oil from escaping and leaves a small interface volume.

subject: Science
question: 6. Collect the next small portion that may contain both liquids and discard it.
answer: Collect the small middle portion (containing both liquids) into a waste container and discard it; this removes the contaminated interface and helps obtain purer layers.

subject: Science
question: 7. Collect the layer of oil separately by opening the stopcock again. You now have two separate liquids. Activity 5.7: Let us explore (camphor sublimation) Activity 5.7. Activity 5.7: Let us explore
answer: After discarding the interface, open the stopcock or carefully decant the remaining oil into a dry container to collect it separately. Activity 5.7 studies camphor sublimation to separate camphor from sand and observe vapour deposition.

subject: Science
question: 1. Take a spatula full of the mixture containing crushed camphor and sand. Put it into a clean and dry china dish. Place it on the tripod stand using a wire gauze.
answer: Put a spatulaful of crushed camphor–sand mixture in a clean, dry china dish, spread it thinly, and place the dish on a tripod with wire gauze for even gentle heating.

subject: Science
question: 2. Take a clean and dry glass funnel. Plug its nozzle with cotton.
answer: Take a clean, dry glass funnel and plug its nozzle loosely with cotton; this stops sand/particles but allows camphor vapour to rise and condense on the funnel.

subject: Science
question: 3. Keep this funnel inverted on the china dish and set up the apparatus as shown in Fig. 5.17.
answer: Invert the plugged funnel over the china dish so the wide end faces down; position it to collect sublimed camphor on the inner surface while vapour rises from the dish.

subject: Science
question: 4. Light the burner and place it under the wire gauze.
answer: Light a burner (spirit lamp or Bunsen) and place it beneath the tripod; use a low to moderate flame so heating is gentle and controlled.

subject: Science
question: 5. Heat the china dish gently for a few minutes.
answer: Heat the china dish gently for a few minutes; camphor will sublime and condense as white crystals on the cooler funnel. Stop heating, let cool, then collect crystals; sand remains in the dish.

subject: Science
question: 6. Observe the inner wall of the funnel carefully. Do you notice any solid deposits?
answer: Yes. You will notice white, solid camphor deposits (sublimed camphor) on the inner wall of the funnel.

subject: Science
question: 7. You may find white, solid camphor deposits on the inner wall of the funnel while sand remains in the china dish.
answer: This occurs because camphor sublimates on heating; its vapour condenses on the cooler inner funnel surface as white solid deposits, while sand remains in the china dish.

subject: Science
question: 6. How Forces Affect Motion
answer: Forces affect motion by changing an object's speed and/or direction. An unbalanced force produces acceleration; balanced forces keep velocity constant.

subject: Science
question: 1. A weightlifter lifts a barbell (Fig. 6.8). List two forces that are acting on the barbell. Are these forces balanced if the weightlifter keeps the barbell steady?
answer: Forces: (1) Gravity (weight) acting downward, (2) Upward muscular/normal force from the lifter. If the barbell is steady these two forces are equal and balanced (net force zero).

subject: Science
question: 10. Suppose a spacecraft is moving in a region of space where the gravitational force acting upon it is negligible. Suggest how can it change its velocity.
answer: By producing thrust: fire engines or thrusters to expel mass (reaction force), use ion thrusters, or contact/propulsive maneuvers (e.g., firing rockets, docking pushes).

subject: Science
question: 2. Two players R and S are participating in an arm-wrestling match (Fig. 6.9). At the instant, when the arms tilt to the front direction (out of the page towards you), are the forces exerted by the players balanced? If not, which player exerted the larger force?
answer: No, the forces are not balanced when the arms tilt. The player whose force causes the forward tilt is exerting the larger force at that instant.

subject: Science
question: 3. An object is moving with a constant velocity. Is there a net force acting upon it?
answer: No. Constant velocity means net force is zero—there is no unbalanced force acting on the object.

subject: Science
question: 4. Suppose, no net force is acting on an object. Which of the following situations are possible? (i) Object remains at rest if at rest. (ii) Object keeps moving with a constant velocity if already moving. (iii) Object is moving with a constant acceleration.
answer: Possible: (i) Object remains at rest if at rest, and (ii) Object keeps moving with constant velocity if already moving. (iii) Moving with constant acceleration is not possible without a net force.

subject: Science
question: 5. In the real world, it is difficult to find a situation where no forces are acting on an object. But by applying additional forces, a condition can be achieved where the net force on the object is zero. Explain with the help of an example.
answer: Example: A book on a table—gravity pulls it down while the table’s normal force upward equals it; net force is zero, so the book stays at rest.

subject: Science
question: 6. A toy car of mass 100 g is moving with a constant velocity of 0.5 m s –1 . What is the net force acting on the toy car?
answer: Net force = 0 N, because the toy car moves with constant velocity (mass 0.1 kg, velocity 0.5 m/s) implying balanced forces.

subject: Science
question: 7. Two children of different masses are sitting on identical swings. To impart identical initial acceleration, for which child would you require to apply a larger force? Explain why.
answer: The heavier child needs a larger force. By Newton’s second law (F = ma), for the same initial acceleration a, force is proportional to mass m, so larger mass requires a larger force.

subject: Science
question: 8. How are glass items packed for transportation using a bubble wrap or hay protected from damage?
answer: Bubble wrap or hay cushions glass by providing soft, compressible layers and air pockets that absorb and distribute shocks, prevent direct impacts and reduce movement and surface-to-surface rubbing during transport.

subject: Science
question: 9. Why does a fireperson sometimes struggle when holding the pipe issuing water? Activity 6.1: Let us investigate (rubber band and coins) Activity 6.1. Activity 6.1: Let us investigate
answer: A fireperson struggles because the water jet produces a backward reaction force (Newton’s third law). High-speed water changes momentum, creating large recoil; holding the pipe needs strength, braces, or teammates to resist that force.

subject: Science
question: 1. Collect four coins of `10, one large strong rubber band and an adhesive tape. Locate horizontal surfaces of different materials, such as wooden table top, cemented floor, laminated table top, and polished marble or tiled floor (you may also choose other surfaces). Check that the surfaces are level.
answer: Collect four 10-rupee coins, a large strong rubber band and adhesive tape. Choose level horizontal surfaces (wooden table, cement floor, laminated top, polished tile) and ensure each surface is clean and level before starting.

subject: Science
question: 2. Stack the four coins on top of each other and secure them together with an adhesive tape around the sides.
answer: Stack the four coins neatly one on another and wrap adhesive tape around their sides firmly so the stack stays together; avoid covering the top and bottom faces to keep them flat.

subject: Science
question: 3. Hold the rubber band slightly stretched between your forefinger and thumb on the wooden table top (Fig. 6.12a). Mark points A and B at its ends as shown in Fig. 6.12b. Make another mark C up to which you will stretch the rubber band.
answer: Place the rubber band slightly stretched on the wooden table and mark its ends A and B. Mark a point C to which you will stretch the band; keep distances measured and fixed for all trials.

subject: Science
question: 4. Holding the ends of the rubber band at A and B, place the stack of coins near the middle of A and B. Now, using a finger of your other hand, push back the stack of coins till the rubber band is pulled back to the mark C (Fig. 6.12c). Then, release the stack of coins and observe its motion. Do you find that after losing contact with the rubber band, the velocity of the stack of coins decreases gradually and it comes to rest after travelling some distance? Measure the distance travelled from C and record it. Repeat this step twice.
answer: Hold the band at A and B, place the taped coin stack midway, pull it back so the band reaches C, release, observe motion and measure distance travelled from C to rest. Repeat twice and record values.

subject: Science
question: 5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 for laminated table top while ensuring that the points A, B and C are marked at the same distances as earlier. Does the stack of coins travel a larger distance than it did on the wooden table top before coming to rest? Does its velocity decrease more slowly now?
answer: Repeat the trial on the laminated tabletop with A, B, C at the same distances. Expect the coins to travel farther and slow down more slowly because the laminated surface has lower friction than wood.

subject: Science
question: 6. Next, repeat step 5 on a horizontal polished marble or tile floor. Does the stack of coins travel an even larger distance and its velocity decrease even more slowly? What conclusion do you draw from your observations? Activity 6.2: Let us measure (spring balance and block) Activity 6.2. Activity 6.2: Let us measure
answer: On polished marble or tile the coins should travel the farthest and decelerate most slowly. Conclusion: smoother surfaces have less friction, so moving objects lose speed more slowly and cover larger distances.

subject: Science
question: 1. Take a spring balance and a wooden block.
answer: Tie the spring balance to the wooden block with a string, check the balance reads zero, and set it to pull the block horizontally; you'll use it to measure the force required to move the block.

subject: Science
question: 2. Place the spring balance in a horizontal position on one of the surfaces used in Activity 6.1 and check that its scale reading is zero. Attach the wooden block to the hook of the spring balance as shown in Fig. 6.14.
answer: Place the spring balance horizontally on the chosen surface, adjust its zero so the scale reads 0, then attach the wooden block to the hook as in Fig. 6.14. Ensure the block rests on the surface without extra force.

subject: Science
question: 3. Pull the spring balance with gradually increasing force and note down the reading on it when the block just starts moving. What does this reading indicate? The forces acting on the block are the force applied by the spring on it and the force of friction. If the velocity of the block is neither increasing nor decreasing, what can you say about the net force acting on the block? Does the reading of the spring balance indicate the magnitude of the force of friction acting on the wooden block?
answer: The reading when the block just starts moving equals the limiting static friction — the applied force needed to overcome static friction. If velocity is constant, net force is zero (forces balanced). Yes: the balance reading equals the frictional force at that instant.

subject: Science
question: 4. Now repeat step 3 on the remaining three surfaces from Activity 6.1.
answer: Repeat the procedure on each of the other three surfaces: place the balance, attach the block, pull gradually and record the spring-balance reading when the block just begins to move for each surface.

subject: Science
question: 5. Compare the readings of the spring balance for all surfaces. Are the readings different? Is the reading smallest for the surface on which the stack of coins travelled the largest distance? Is the reading largest for which the distance travelled was the smallest? Activity 6.3: Let us experiment (cart, pulley, varying force) Activity 6.3. Activity 6.3: Let us experiment (Demonstration activity)
answer: Readings will differ. Smoother surfaces give smaller readings (lower friction) and larger coin travel distances; rougher surfaces give larger readings and shorter distances. So smallest reading corresponds to largest distance travelled, largest reading to smallest distance.

subject: Science
question: 1. Take four ball bearing wheels, two pencils, an empty cardboard box (to make a cart), a paper cup, a piece of pipe (to use as a pulley), a length of thread, some coins or other objects (to place in cup) and a weighing scale to measure mass.
answer: Gather four ball-bearing wheels, two pencils, an empty cardboard box (cart), a paper cup, a short pipe (pulley), thread, coins/weights, and a weighing scale — these form the cart, pulley and hanging mass for the experiment.

subject: Science
question: 2. Insert two pencils through the sides of the box near the bottom, to function as axles and attach a wheel to each of their free ends as shown in Fig. 6.17a (if the wheels are loose, wrap some adhesive tape at the pencil ends to fit the wheels tightly). Attach a thread to the front end of the box with which you can pull the cart.
answer: Insert the two pencils through the box sides near the bottom as axles, fit a wheel on each exposed pencil end (use tape to secure loose wheels). Attach a thread to the front of the box to pull the cart.

subject: Science
question: 3. Draw a line at one end of the table, which will mark the starting point for the cart. Put the thread over a small pipe attached at the other end of the table (Fig. 6.17b). To this thread attach a cup in which you can put some objects. As you let the system go, the cup will move down due to the gravitational force by the Earth on it, and the thread will pull the cart with a constant force.
answer: Draw the start line at one table end. Pass the thread over the pipe at the other end and attach the cup to the hanging end. When released, the cup’s weight pulls the cart with an approximately constant force.

subject: Science
question: 4. Measure the mass of the cup along with any other objects put inside it with the weighing scale.
answer: Weigh the paper cup together with any objects placed inside using the weighing scale and record the mass accurately; this mass determines the pulling force (weight = mass × g).

subject: Science
question: 5. Start recording a video of the cart in slow motion. Release the cart from the start line, and record the video until it reaches the pipe at the other end of the table.
answer: Start slow-motion recording before release, keep the camera stable and include the start line and pipe in frame. Release the cart and record until it reaches the pipe, saving the footage for time analysis.

subject: Science
question: 6. Read the time when you released the cart and when it reached the end of the table by seeing the slow-motion video, and record the difference as time T1.
answer: From the slow-motion video, note the timestamp or frame at release and at arrival; the difference is T1. If using frames, T1 = (frame_end − frame_start) / frame_rate. Record T1 with its units (seconds).

subject: Science
question: 7. Now double the mass of the cup with the objects inside it, and repeat steps 5 and 6 to record the time difference T2. Using the values of the time measured, let us do some analysis. For both cases, the cart starts with zero velocity u = 0 and travels the same distance s. If a1 and a2 are the accelerations in the two cases respectively, using kinematic equation, we obtain s = 1/2 a1 T1^2 and s = 1/2 a2 T2^2. Equating the two equations, we obtain a2/a1 = (T1/T2)^2. Substituting the values of T1 and T2, you find that when you increased the force for the same mass of the cart, the acceleration increased. You may conclude that the acceleration of an object of fixed mass increases as the net force applied on it increases. Activity 6.4: Let us experiment (double mass of cart) Activity 6.4. Activity 6.4: Let us experiment (Demonstration activity)
answer: a2/a1 = (T1/T2)^2. Substituting measured T1 and T2 shows a increased when force increased for the same mass. Conclusion: for fixed mass, acceleration increases as net force increases (a ∝ F).

subject: Science
question: 1. Repeat Activity 6.3 with a variation. Keep the mass of the cup and objects inside it constant. Double the mass of the cart by adding more objects in it.
answer: Method: keep cup+objects mass constant. Double cart mass by adding known extra weights. Use same pull and release from rest over the same distance; measure time. Expect longer time and smaller acceleration for the heavier cart.

subject: Science
question: 2. Measure the mass of the cart along with the objects inside it with a weighing scale.
answer: Place the cart (with cup and objects) on a zeroed weighing scale. Record the mass in kg (or g). Repeat 2–3 times and take the average; report the total mass with units and any small variation.

subject: Science
question: 3. Carry out steps 5 and 6 of Activity 6.3. Using the values of time measured, find the ratio of acceleration for these two cases. Do you find that for the same force, when you increased the mass of the cart, the acceleration decreased? This means that for a given magnitude of a force, the acceleration produced is inversely related to the mass of the object. Activity 6.6: Let us verify (two spring balances) Activity 6.6. Activity 6.6: Let us verify
answer: Calculate a1 = 2s/T1^2 and a2 = 2s/T2^2; ratio a2/a1 = (T1/T2)^2. When mass is doubled with same force, T increases and acceleration decreases. Conclusion: for same F, a ∝ 1/m (Newton’s second law).

subject: Science
question: 1. Take two identical spring balances.
answer: Take two identical spring balances, hook them together and fix one end. Prediction: when stationary, both balances read the same value equal to the applied pull, because tension is the same throughout.

subject: Science
question: 2. Place them in horizontal position on a table and connect them by their hooks as shown in Fig. 6.26. Fix the free end of one of the spring balances to an immovable object or hold it fixed by your hand.
answer: Place balances horizontally, connect hooks, and fix one free end to a support. When you pull the other free end, both scales show equal readings since the tension in the connection is uniform.

subject: Science
question: 3. Imagine that you are pulling the free end of the other spring balance with your other hand. Predict what will be the readings of their scales if the spring balances are stationary.
answer: Prediction: both spring balances will show identical readings equal to the magnitude of the force you apply, because the stationary system has the same tension throughout.

subject: Science
question: 4. Now, carry out step 3. Repeat it multiple times by varying the magnitude of the force applied by you. Is your observation same as your prediction? Activity 6.7: Let us understand (balloon rocket) Activity 6.7. Activity 6.7: Let us understand
answer: Observation: readings match the prediction — both scales read the same value and increase together as you pull harder. Small differences may appear due to friction or instrument inaccuracy.

subject: Science
question: 1. Collect a large balloon, a piece of drinking straw, adhesive tape, a long thread, and two nails or hooks on two walls.
answer: Collect a large balloon, a drinking straw, adhesive tape, a long thread, and two wall nails/hooks. Thread the string between the nails, tape the straw to the balloon to act as a slider, and mount on the string.

subject: Science
question: 2. Inflate the balloon and tie its neck with a small piece of thread.
answer: Inflate the balloon and tie its neck with thread. Tape the straw along the balloon, place the straw on the stretched string between hooks, hold the balloon’s neck, then release to see it move along the string by expelled air (action–reaction).

subject: Science
question: 3. Stick the piece of straw with an adhesive tape on the surface of the balloon such that, one end of the straw points towards the neck of the balloon, as shown in Fig. 6.29.
answer: Stick the straw flat on the balloon with tape so one open end points toward the neck; the straw acts as a low-friction guide and directs the escaping air through its open end for a smoother jet.

subject: Science
question: 4. Pass the thread through the straw and tie its two ends to the nails, keeping the thread taut (Fig. 6.29).
answer: Pass a long thread through the straw and tie its ends to two fixed nails so the thread is taut and horizontal. The straw will slide along the taut thread when the balloon moves.

subject: Science
question: 5. Remove the thread tied to the neck of the balloon and observe in which direction the straw and the balloon move. Explain the motion in terms of Newton's third law.
answer: On release the air jets backward; by Newton's third law the balloon + straw are pushed forward along the thread (action: air expelled backward; reaction: forward push on the balloon).

subject: Science
question: 7. Work, Energy, and Simple Machines
